author: milesdeutscher
quoted_text:
My thoughts on the current state of crypto/markets (and what's next):

• In general, the world is in a volatile/scary place right now. Cyberattacks, FAA flight chaos, etc. I think people are really starting to worry about where they can store capital (this thesis is backed by the general stock market dip)
• In hindsight, the Binance hack was a huge bear signal for crypto. Stablecoin supply fell 5%+ after the hack. Whenever this happens, it's typically a huge bear signal for crypto and liquidity flowing out. This trust takes a while to rebuild and there is usually a delayed reaction which we are seeing now.
• Crypto ran on the debasement narrative. Now the narrative has shifted to the AI buildout struggling/growth fears, and that's weighing on every macro asset.
• The breakout to the 80s was a classic bull trap (deviation above range high). I think a lot of people got trapped. For me, losing the $74K range low was the real bear signal in terms of market structure. There is major support at $60k. Expecting this to hold, but if it doesn't things would get very ugly (not my base case for now).
• My $BTC plan: wait for an uptrend to form on the 4H and look for a swing into the high 70s. If not, I'll bid on the weekly timeframe close to $60K with inval below. Breaking $60K would be like breaking $40K in 2022: pure capitulation.
• For a real move back to the upside, we'd need a meaningful pivot in monetary policy. That can happen, but right now the Fed is hawkish (and only getting more so).
• All eyes on macro/equities rn. If stocks are weak, BTC/crypto is going to struggle (most of the relative strength is gone now - a big reason being the Binance hack)
• In terms of alts, I'm only really interested in laddering into $BTC, $HYPE & $ZEC. I also think these take time but from a long term POV I think they are solid assets to DCA and hold. There are 5-6 other assets I'm interested in, but until the overall market stabilizes they're relatively uninvestable imo (unless you're willing to cop big downside). Overall, I'd say we're closer to the bottom now, but that doesn't necessarily R/R favours heavily deploying here. As I said before I'd rather wait for some strength than catch a knife (with the exception of some light long term DCAs).
• From a business POV, I'm 90% focused on AI now. Imo, building a business is always the best hedge against volatile markets. There is so much opportunity there, which is exciting. And automated trading of course. There's going to be a massive shift in financial markets with agents, and it's a very fun intersection to build in.
• Advice: don't trade shaky markets. Just focus on upskilling and increasing active income to trade in better market conditions. But also don't be afraid to take advantage of asymmetric opportunities if they present.

最近半导体的主线，是反弹空。

1958年以来的 17次中期选举，标普在选后六个月，全部实现正收益。

选后六个月内 ，最大回撤超过 5%的只有 3次。

18年持续加息，叠加中美贸易战。

选后约一个半月，标普下跌 14.7%，12月24日见底。

19年2月15日收复选举日点位，选后六个月累计上涨4.6%。
————
02年科技泡沫，叠加伊拉克战争风险。

选后调整四个月，03年3月11日最大回撤 12.5%。

4月23日收复了选举日的点位，选后六个月累计上涨0.5%。
————
当前经济暂时没有衰退信号。

就是因为当前经济仍有韧性，叠加了通胀，反而加息直接对市场造成压力。
————
利率期货定价，12月加息 25个基点的概率，约80%，到2027年7月，累计加息 50个基点的概率约 84%。

这与美联储点阵图有分歧，也是市场未来会震荡的一个重要原因。 

就是当前大家对加息的定价，是不充分的。
————
当前半导体交易主线是信贷、资金成本和杠杆出清。

美国10年期国债收益率仍高，高收益债信用利差扩大至348个基点。

高利率提高数据中心的融资成本，信用利差扩大进一步抬高Neocloud等企业的借款成本。

加上 Anthropic IPO 估值一降再降，市场对 AI 资本开支的回报产生怀疑，让半导体本就在一个杀市值的状态里。
——————
结果，

11月3日中选之后，

41项与数据中心有关的地方投票中，40项结果倾向限制数据中心开发。

民主党新当选的得州州长还提出，暂停批准新的数据中心项目，直到州议会出台相关监管措施。
————

半导体此前已经计入极高的增长预期。

仓位拥挤和杠杆进一步放大了跌幅。

6月30日至11月3日，半导体未来盈利预期上调30%，远期市盈率却下降35%。

高增长预期、集中持仓和杠杆交易，使利空更容易引发连锁抛售。
————
如果数据中心监管导致资本开支和半导体盈利预期下修，市场还可能出现第二轮下跌。

不管怎么样，还是应该等纳指或者费城半导体突破EMA21，并回踩不破，再看多不迟。

text:
So Diogo Almeida is one of the most fascinating CEOs I have ever interviewed.

born in the Philippines

2008: wins bronze for the Philippines at the International Mathematical Olympiad

2013: starts his career as a software engineer at Amazon

2017: joins Google Brain, working on cutting-edge deep learning research

2018: leaves Google Brain and takes roughly 18 months off to figure out what makes him happy

travels the world, experiments with improv, art and meditation

becomes a top-30 League of Legends player

discovers that none of it makes him particularly happy

2020: joins OpenAI when it's still a relatively obscure research laboratory

helps develop reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), the technique that transforms how people interact with AI

2022: co-authors the landmark InstructGPT paper

the work becomes foundational to ChatGPT

November 2022: ChatGPT launches and becomes one of the fastest-growing consumer products in history

2023: contributes to GPT-4, one of the most important model releases in AI history

but starts questioning the fundamental assumptions behind the technology he helped build

2024: leaves OpenAI while ChatGPT is exploding in popularity

people think he's crazy for walking away

co-founds TypeSafe AI with Erik Gafni and Sasha Sheng

spends two years in stealth developing an entirely new class of AI models

September 15, 2026: launches Jev, TypeSafe's first System One model

Company makes $100M in revenue in the first 7 days of launch

raises a reported $40M seed round led by DCVC

October 2026: a reported $870M Series A at a $7.5B valuation, backed by a16z

argues that the next breakthrough in AI will come from making intelligence cheap, reliable and autonomous

My notes from my discussion with @CompleteSkeptic below:

1. Why Jevons' Paradox Does Not Cut It. We Are Going to 10x That

Diogo expects a "mega Jevons paradox", with usage that dwarfs the token consumption of LLMs and AI running in the background everywhere. He expects people to stop seeing AI as something that "slops crap at them" and start seeing it as something that makes life better.

2. Why SaaS Incumbents Are Better Positioned Than OpenAI and Anthropic in Many Application Spaces

SaaS companies know their customers' workflows and have the scale to fund the upfront engineering that real automation requires. Diogo argues their edge comes from being closest to the problems, not from distribution. Teams inside products like TurboTax know where to improve the interface, while OpenAI and Anthropic are "still living in their ivory tower."

3. Why We Do Not Hire From OpenAI

Diogo sees getting into OpenAI as an anti-signal and says its researchers love algorithms and scaling but hate data. Data is a low-status topic at most labs, and the few people focused on the right task would want to pursue their own. That leaves researchers obsessed with algorithms, which he likens to throwing money in the furnace.

4. How the AI Bubble Could Burst and Where the Demand Shock Could Be

Part of today's AI demand is driven by FOMO, from people believing they are getting good results. Diogo finds many buyers miscalibrated and overestimating what AI can do. Once they face the realities of its capabilities, demand could fall quickly.

5. What Metric Did ChatGPT Optimize for in the Early Days?

Before Claude Code, ChatGPT was optimized for monthly active users rather than the best chatbot experience, which is how sycophancy emerged. Companies are now optimizing for the MAU equivalent in coding agents. Without a dedicated model, Diogo doubts they will produce a comparable one soon.

6. Why the Talent Market Is Not Crazy for Us and We Don't Pay for Mercenaries

TypeSafe pays people good amounts but not the highest, which filters out hired guns. Diogo says Anthropic is suffering from mercenaries because it pays more than anyone else, and an entire market now exists to prepare candidates for Anthropic culture interviews.

7. We Wanted Sonya Huang More Than We Wanted Sequoia

Diogo did not want Sequoia's money and brought the firm in because of Sonya. He values her particular shape of brilliance, which offers a perspective no other advisor gives him. One TypeSafe value is to make great decisions slowly, and he sees her as a valuable thought partner for that.

text:
Calibration - the probabilities provided by a decision model are only useful if they're correct. When it says 80%, it should be right about 80% of the time, which lets you set a threshold. For example, you can automatically send tasks where the model has low confidence to human review.

Calibration error measures the gap between a model's predicted probability and how often it is right. Across 13 benchmarks and 22,505 questions answered by all five models, d1.2-ultra's calibration error is 0.8 points, compared with 1.2 for d1.2, 2.7 for Jev 1.14, 3.7 for Perplexity's Decider v1.3, and 7.2 for GPT-6 Luna on its Decisions API.

text:
Lighter $15.5m hack. explained for dummies

tldr: exploit of the community pools feature. the protocol wasn't hacked. smart contracts are intact. a couple of people affected. in theory anyone whose api keys got stolen was at risk for a while. should be fine now

two big market makers had their api keys leaked

here are the victims' addresses (possibly wallets of the Abraxas Capital fund):

0x0d1D09312665D31Ed68231b88079a245E0458F6F - 10,383,864.27 USDC

0x66Cf2f85115CC20bF439720927C1f93De9672068 - 5,086,895.71 USDC (but these didn't make it out)

you probably know what an API key is, but still. it's a key "for the bot": it can trade and even withdraw, but only to the owner's own wallet. sending funds to anyone else needs a signature from the main wallet. so the worst case should be dumping your positions, right?

but Lighter has public pools: a shared vault account run by a trader, where other people put money in and get shares. any account can create a pool. with an API key. no wallet signature. and that's exactly how the money got pulled out.

HOW?

let's go step by step:

1) what's an account on Lighter? 

it's a record in Lighter's l2 database with a number (account_index), a USDC balance and positions. tied to an L1 address (an Ethereum wallet). one L1 address can have several accounts: a main one and sub-accounts. controlled by an API key (trading, sub-accounts) and an L1 key (transfers to others, changing api keys)

2) what's a pool? 

you probably know it's basically copytrading behind the pool leader. technically it's the same account, just with the "pool" type (account_type 2) and a share table: who holds what percent of the pool. created via create_public_pool(operator_fee, initial_total_shares, min_operator_share_rate) from the main account, and the pool gets its L1 address. the operator trades the pool with their API key

3) how a normal (regular, via ui) pool deposit works

one call: mint_shares(public_pool_index, share_amount) from the depositor's account. the sequencer: computes share price = pool balance / number of shares → debits share_amount × price usdc from the depositor → credits it to the pool → increases the share count and records share_amount to the depositor. money and shares change in one operation, the ratio holds

4) how the hacker's deposit went

not mint_shares, but transfer in same_master_account mode: from victim account #714710 to pool account #281474976415757 in $1m chunks. to the sequencer it's a transfer between two accounts under the same L1 address, no L1 signature. it credits USDC to the pool and that's it. the share table is untouched.

so the hacker's account held ±100% of the pool's shares. the pool's NAV spiked, and every one of the hacker's shares got worth multiples more. and the victim, due to the technical vulnerability, held only about 0.01%

here's drainer pool 1 - https://t.co/OBIzGvOmMz
here's drainer pool 2 - https://t.co/sZNZKBUEPc

and here's where the $10m from pool 1 was pulled out to - 0xb3fffca23d4444ee73349825acd84f7b5020e387

text:
I think the people who think a successful $ANT IPO will save the neoclouds and semis are wrong.

The problem with neoclouds was always their business model. They are a phenomenon of a compute shortage and a low-AI financing-debt environment. Without those two conditions, they can't compete with the hyperscalers because building data centers is a scale game, and reaching scale requires funds. $NVDA being the financing bank of the neoclouds has only extended the life of many of the neoclouds, but the problem stays; the business model for most is just bad.

$ANT is also not going to save the space, as $ANT, without a significant uptick in usage (like they saw in 2026, when coding exploded and wasn't expected by them ), will not do pricey spot compute deals. $ANT will do long-term compute deals with heavy discounts and attractive pricing for them, as they are the biggest buyer on the market.

For you to service a long-term deal data center deal with $ANT, their economics require you to have a low cost of capital, and the low-cost capital market is basically closed for the neoclouds. $ANT is also not stupid to make big prepayments for data centers, or if they do that, the economics of these neoclouds will be even worse, as $ANT holds all the negotiating cards.

Also, don't get me wrong; I think $ANT will have a successful IPO, but it won't "save" that portion of the market.

The AI buildout will continue, but at a more normal pace, with the strongest and healthiest companies leading it ( $AMZN, $MSFT, $GOOGL, and $META) and with a semis mix of TPUs, Trainiums, $AMD, $NVDA, and many other ASICs. The chip design layer margin will shrink, and you will get more compute out of your investment.

Anthropic 价差这两天基本没有了，今天已经停止，下一个跨所套利机会在哪？我昨天开始扫了 394 对。

思路很简单：同一个资产在多个交易所都有永续，只要两边没有硬锚、资金不互通，价格就会各走各的，价差能偏很久，等它回来就是利润。

扫描范围：Hyperliquid 全部 dex（含 Entropy 的 io、xyz、para）、Lighter 主网 / Robinhood 链、Arcus，共 394 对同名标的。每 10 秒记一次两边的买一卖一和吃深度均价，再按实盘规则回测。

24 小时回测结果（样本还小，仅供参考）：

🟢 NVDA：Arcus × Entropy(io)：5 轮，每天约 +$14（每腿 $2000）。两边都计积分，最值得盯（但又马上财报所以风险又很大）

🟡 UNITREE（宇树）：xyz / para × Lighter，价差波动最大（标准差 8–9bp），但盘口太薄，扣完成本几乎不赚

🟡 OPENAI：io × Lighter，结构和 ANT 一样，但这一天很安静，只出现 1 次机会

📉 接下来会把 NVDA 和 OPENAI 再采 2–3 天，避开财报。看看数据情况决定是否上实盘。

text:
Vitalik just flipped to “total bull” on leanPCS via EIP-8288.

The core idea: aggregate STARKs, quantum-safe signatures, and other heavy proofs in the mempool so the chain only sees small claim hashes + one master proof instead of the full bulky objects.

This is aimed at hyper-scaling data and execution for things that only need to be computed once (signatures, STARKs, Merkle branches, FHE, etc.), especially once we go post-quantum and those objects get much larger.

If this lands and gets used, the impact should show up in onchain data. Here are the growthepie metrics worth watching and why:

1. Rent Paid to L1 / Onchain Profit (Economics page)
This is the direct measure of what L2s currently pay Ethereum to post their data + verification proofs/states. EIP-8288 specifically targets shrinking the proof and signature verification portion of that cost. If aggregation works as intended, this line should improve (or grow more slowly) relative to L2 activity, particularly for ZK rollups.

2. Data Availability metrics (data posted + fees across Ethereum Blobs vs. Celestia/EigenDA)
Shows how much data is still landing on Ethereum versus alternative DA layers. 8288 doesn’t replace blob scaling, but it reduces the onchain footprint of the proofs and signatures that accompany the data. Watch whether Ethereum’s share of DA stays high while the cost per unit of useful computation falls.

3. Throughput (gas used per second)
Measures actual computational work happening across the ecosystem. Cheaper verification of heavy operations should raise the amount of real execution that can fit before hitting gas or data limits. Sustained increases in throughput alongside stable or falling settlement costs would be a strong signal.

4. Fees paid / transaction costs (chain and application level)
Useful as a secondary check. If verification of complex crypto becomes dramatically cheaper, you should eventually see that reflected in lower effective costs for privacy protocols, account abstraction, multisigs, and any L2s that rely on heavy proofs.

These won’t move immediately - EIP-8288 is still a draft, but they’re the cleanest public metrics for tracking whether the “cryptographic proof singularity” path actually reduces settlement friction and unlocks more scale.

Primary places to watch:
- https://t.co/ZOASHg4Sph
- https://t.co/7OvR13yL8z
- https://t.co/HkLfpYupsu
- https://t.co/ARk0XNUEoD
- https://t.co/l64yybLBWj
author: growthepie_eth
quoted_text:
Over the past few weeks I've gone from thinking leanPCS is total bull to being a total bull. So let me explain some of these buzzwords in more detail.

At the core, 8288 is about hyper-scaling data and execution for any computation that needs to get performed on a piece of data once, the chain learns the answer, and then we never need to see that data again. This sounds very specific, but it includes most "heavy" things happening on Ethereum:

* Signatures
* STARKs
* Merkle branches
* FHE computation
* ...

Really the first two are the most important.

Once we go quantum-safe, signatures get bigger (65 bytes ECDSA -> 1-6 kB WOTS/SPHINCS depending on params) and ZKPs get much bigger (200-1000 bytes with groth16, PLONK, etc -> 128 kB with STARKs). This is unsustainable to put on chain, and 8288 fixes this.

8288 works by aggregating STARKs in the mempool. First, you as a user generate the STARK or SPHINCS signature or PCS opening (more on that last one later), and publish it. Then, each node listens. Each tick, each node takes all of the new objects that it has seen, and generates a STARK containing a list of "claims":

"pubkey P has signed message M"
"program X run on data D has output Y"
"p(X) = Y for some polynomial P whose hash is H"

and a proof that it has seen a signature, STARK or PCS opening verifying those claims. So the only information getting re-broadcasted is:

(i) hashes of inputs and outputs (~64-96 bytes per claim)
(ii) a single STARK proof per tick

These aggregate proofs themselves get re-aggregated, and eventually you get to a single "master proof" in the block, that verifies that all of those statements are true. And so the only other data that has to actually go on chain is the statements (the (P, M), (X, D, Y), (X, Y, H) tuples I described above), not the actual signatures or proofs. This gets put into a specialized frame type.

Now, let's get into the leanSPHINCS vs leanSTARK vs leanPCS part.

The core distinction is: *what is the underlying object that the user is creating?*

In leanSPHINCS, it's a signature, and specifically this particular type of purely-hash-based signature: https://t.co/HOazliHq9N

If we add leanSPHINCS, then users will be able to make quantum-safe accounts, and pay only a little bit of gas (4096 for the 64 bytes) for each signature. So we get scalable quantum-safety for regular accounts, multisigs, etc. But it's only one specific signature scheme, you can't do anything else.

In leanSTARK, it's a STARK. This means it's fully general: the user runs whatever computation they want, and publish a STARK of it. So you can use it for:

* Any signature scheme (including eg. lattice-based ones if you like those)
* A multisig that hides its internal logic
* Privacy protocols
* Private account abstraction: authorization logic that depends on some value hidden elsewhere in the state, so you can have one key that controls all your accounts without publicly linking them to each other

Basically, it's a free for all, in the same way the EVM is a free for all.

But leanSTARK has a practical downside. The protocol would have to specify the language in which users write their programs (we call this the "ISA"). So we would have to agree on that language. This is a really big deal - it's the first big case of "Ethereum moving beyond the EVM" - and so it's likely to take time to agree on the details of it, especially since the ISA would be hard to upgrade. There are benefits to taking longer on this, figuring out the ideal ISA, and then even giving access to it inside regular contracts.

LeanPCS is the third option. PCS stands for "polynomial commitment scheme": a proof that P(x) = y. The most important thing to know about PCSes is that they are by far the most important "hard" component of a STARK (see here: https://t.co/EEQWMU0gAf ). If you have a "magic PCS oracle" (which from the EVM's point of view, 8288 is), you can verify a STARK in ~20-40k gas.

The most important gain with PCS is that there is far less that we need to choose. Specifying a PCS only requires specifying a field, and there is a natural option: the 128 bit binary field (technically, we can go more general than that, and say the 2^k-bit binary recursive tower field, going up to 256)

LeanPCS is less efficient than leanSTARK onchain, because you would have to put multiple claims to prove one thing. But it's arguably more efficient offchain, because you have much more flexibility to choose proof systems.

But most importantly, leanPCS gives you the same generality as leanSTARK, in a way that could potentially be implemented very quickly. And once we figure out the ISA, we can add leanSTARK later.

So there is a route to getting "the cryptographic proof singularity" much faster than any of us expected, and that route runs through 8288 with leanPCS.

author: donovanchoy
quoted_text:
SANC Buyback and Burn Announcement

Sanctum recently concluded buybacks of solana:CLoUDKc4Ane7HeQcPpE3YHnznRxhMimJ4MyaUqyHFzAu.

10,708,333 solana:CLoUDKc4Ane7HeQcPpE3YHnznRxhMimJ4MyaUqyHFzAu was bought back at an average price of $0.0261. That is about 2.43% of current circulating supply.

We have burned them: https://t.co/OJypQtOksx

The current circulating supply is 460,125,448 solana:CLoUDKc4Ane7HeQcPpE3YHnznRxhMimJ4MyaUqyHFzAu. You can view the full breakdown on our investor relations dashboard: https://t.co/ZumhIwaRvI

Why did we buy back solana:CLoUDKc4Ane7HeQcPpE3YHnznRxhMimJ4MyaUqyHFzAu?
Crypto as an industry is in an unusual position. When you buy a company’s shares, the law gives you rights: you can vote for the board, hold directors to account, and claim a portion of what’s left if the company is sold or wound down. Tokenholders have no such rights. Without a legal claim on the business, buybacks are one of the few ways the value a protocol creates can reach its tokenholders directly.

However, for an early-stage company, every dollar spent buying tokens is a dollar not spent on hiring, product development, or growth. A young company in most other industries would rarely use its cash this way.

We don’t think buybacks should be a default. They make sense only when they’re the highest-return use of our capital. This is often, though not always, the case when a token’s market cap is low relative to the protocol’s expected future cash flows. In June, SANC’s market cap fell below $7 million, at one point trading close to the value of our treasury. In effect, the market was pricing the business itself at nearly zero despite our products and our revenue. We thought that was wrong, so we began buying back tokens.

Why burn the solana:CLoUDKc4Ane7HeQcPpE3YHnznRxhMimJ4MyaUqyHFzAu?
We considered holding the bought-back solana:CLoUDKc4Ane7HeQcPpE3YHnznRxhMimJ4MyaUqyHFzAu in the Strategic Reserve to preserve optionality. But the reserve is already sufficient for grants, incentives, and team compensation for the foreseeable future. While we’ve never sold from the reserve despite multiple OTC offers, we may do so in the future if it’s in the protocol’s long-term interest. Burning makes the buyback irreversible: those tokens can never return to the market.

Will there be future buybacks?
We have no fixed buyback program. This buyback was done on a discretionary basis and we may or may not do so again in the future.

Addendum: Update to Circulating Supply
We previously declared our circulating supply assuming full distribution to team and investors (250M team + 130M investors). However, since some of the buybacks came from departing team members and investors, that is no longer accurate.

In the interests of transparency, we will calculate circulating supply directly from on-chain data with three carveouts:

1. We count vested-but-unclaimed tokens in the Magna vesting contract as circulating.
2. One investor’s 30M solana:CLoUDKc4Ane7HeQcPpE3YHnznRxhMimJ4MyaUqyHFzAu vests through Anchorage rather than Magna, so it isn’t visible as locked on-chain. We manually exclude the still-locked portion.
3. We hold 15M solana:CLoUDKc4Ane7HeQcPpE3YHnznRxhMimJ4MyaUqyHFzAu in the Strategic Reserve on behalf of an investor who hasn’t provided a claim address. We manually include the unlocked portion as circulating, since it belongs to them and not to Sanctum.

The accurate circulating supply calculation can be found at https://t.co/ZumhIwaRvI

text:
🚨 $SOFI: THIS IS BIG. SOFIUSD LANDS ON POLYGON.

SOFI COULD NOW POWER PAYMENTS FOR BUSINESSES THAT HAVE NEVER OPENED A SOFI ACCOUNT.

Crazy and I didn't expect it to come this early.

A few of you see this as another stablecoin launching on another blockchain.

I think $SoFi is trying to become the bank behind payment platforms that don't want to become banks themselves. ♥️

Polygon already has the infrastructure for wallets, fiat conversions, cross-border payments, compliance and settlement. Businesses can integrate these services without building the entire financial stack themselves.

Now SoFiUSD is available inside that infrastructure alongside USDC, USDT and PYUSD. A merchant doesn't need to use SoFi's banking app for SoFi to become part of its payment infrastructure.

A fintech could use Polygon to move customer funds, settle transactions or make international payouts while using SoFiUSD as the underlying digital dollar.

The merchant keeps its customer relationship. Polygon provides the payment infrastructure. SoFi Bank issues the dollar being transferred.

It's a very different business opportunity from simply getting more people to open SoFi accounts. Stablecoin transaction volume and stablecoin balances are two different businesses.

A dollar can move between businesses hundreds of times without creating hundreds of dollars of stablecoin balances.

The payment activity creates potential opportunities for transaction services, distribution and enterprise relationships. But the outstanding stablecoin balance is what determines the size of the reserve assets backing the tokens.

If SoFiUSD achieves circulation, the reserve economics will become valuable, subject to regulation, asset yields and operating costs.

Don't foget that $SoFi already owns something most stablecoin startups don't : 

A nationally chartered bank. 😍

Galileo already provides financial technology infrastructure to other businesses. SoFi could eventually offer issuing, banking services, payments and blockchain settlement through a broader enterprise relationship.

The integration is not announced in the Polygon release but commercially, I think it's one of the more interesting possibilities.

What really caught my attention is Polygon's statement that businesses already settling on its network can use SoFiUSD without building a new integration.

SoFi doesn't have to convince millions of merchants to integrate directly with SoFi. It can compete for their payment flows through infrastructure they already use.

That's how distribution can become more important than the stablecoin launch itself.

Jensen Huang is discussing a COMEBACK as "Nvidia CEO" with allies, who are lobbying the board and seeking White House support, the FT reports.

He resigned on November 12 following reports of affairs with a subordinate and a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

A petition to bring him back as CEO has now surpassed 120,000 signatures.

But his resignation has divided opinion, drawing support from prominent investors and scrutiny from lawmakers.

Here’s what leaders in tech, finance and Washington have said:

1. Donald Trump, U.S. president — Said Huang is “going through hell,” reportedly urged him to stay, and floated Tim Cook as his replacement.

2. Elon Musk, Tesla and SpaceX CEO — Said hiring Huang “would be an honor” and confirmed signing the petition.

3. Changpeng “CZ” Zhao, Binance co-founder — “It’s a mistake for Nvidia to let Jensen resign.”

4. Scott Bessent, U.S. Treasury secretary — Criticised Commerce for failing to blacklist Megaspeed and questioned Nvidia’s sales to apparent shell companies.

5. Todd Blanche, U.S. attorney general — Said the FBI is investigating and has not determined whether Alice Huang was a spy.

6. Tim Scott, Republican senator and Senate Banking Committee chair — Asked Huang and Howard Lutnick to testify on December 3.

7. Brian Mast, Republican congressman and House Foreign Affairs Committee chair — Stressed Nvidia’s importance to America despite his disagreements with Huang.

8. Hakeem Jeffries, House Democratic leader — Welcomed the resignation but said national security concerns remain.

9. Pete Ricketts, Republican senator — Said the resignation “does not absolve Nvidia” from a full investigation.

10. Chuck Schumer, Democratic senator — Said Congress must still demand answers from Huang and Nvidia.

11. Scott Wiener, Democratic congressman-elect from San Francisco — Called for AI regulation and answers about information potentially reaching China.

12. Bill Ackman, Pershing Square founder — “Even incredible humans make mistakes.” Urged support for Huang and his family.

13. Shaun Maguire, Sequoia Capital partner — Called Huang irreplaceable for American AI leadership while criticising his conduct.

14. Gavin Baker, Atreides Management founder — Warned that losing Huang would be “a disaster for America—and a gift to China.”

15. Sarah Guo, Conviction AI VC founder — “Sadly, greatness doesn’t guarantee goodness.”

16. David Sacks, investor — Suggested Huang’s support for open-source AI contributed to his exit. That remains their theory.

17. Lloyd Blankfein, former Goldman Sachs CEO — Compared Huang to Shakespeare’s tragic characters.

18. Stephen Witt, Huang’s biographer — Said Huang made those around him so wealthy that eventually “no one could say no to him.”

19. Jim Cramer, CNBC host — Said Huang “let me down.”

20. Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker from investment firms — Asked the board to keep Huang’s potential return on the table.

Opinions are divided. Now, a possible comeback is taking shape.

Another BIG WEEK ahead for Nvidia.

text:
这是个大雷啊💣

黑客袭击别人，作为 DeFi 借贷老大的 AAVE 
却得背锅还债

DeFi 该咋 De？

10 月 29 日，币安热钱包被盗 63 亿美元

同一天，一个跟这起案子相关的钱包，把 6000 万 USDT 存进 Aave

三分钟，借走 19,762 枚 WETH，当时值 4460 万美元

这是一次洗钱换仓

USDT 是 Tether 一个指令就能冻结的资产，ETH 不是

黑客用 Aave 当通道，把能被冻的钱，换成了不能被冻的钱

Aave 的守护者 40 分钟后冻结市场

11 月 4 日，清算人还了 9,884 枚 WETH，拿走 2,438 万 USDT

账还没清完

到 11 月 5 日，还欠 9,885 枚 WETH，抵押 3,557 万 USDT，健康系数 1.24

这笔账最后会落在谁头上

两种结局

第一种，ETH 涨 24% 以上，这个仓位再次可清算，清算人接走抵押品，Aave 全身而退

第二种，Tether 冻结那 3,557 万 USDT

抵押品归零，债务还在，没人接盘，坏账落在 Aave 的存款人头上

一个跟 Aave 毫无关系的黑客事件，最后可能是 Aave 的用户买单

这就是背锅还债的完整链条

这不是第一次

3 月 10 日，Aave 的 CAPO 价格预言机配置出错，34 个仓位被误清算，2,700 万美元

4 月，KelpDAO 的 LayerZero 桥被攻破 2.92 亿美元

48 小时，Aave 流出 84.5 亿美元存款

DAO 最后拿出约 3 亿美元救助

三次事件，只有一次是 Aave 自己的代码出问题

另外两次，一次是交易所被黑，一次是别人的桥被攻破

问题出在 V3 的设计

V3 是共享资金池

所有抵押品放在一个池子里，一套风险参数

rsETH 出事，WETH 的存款人一起承担

osETH 被杠杆玩到 14 倍，稳定币的存款人一起承担

11 月 9 日，LlamaRisk 提案，把 13.3 亿美元抵押品、10.3 亿美元债务踢出新敞口

rsETH 抵押 6.618 亿，债务 6.057 亿

osETH 抵押 2.794 亿，债务 2.566 亿

LBTC 1.774 亿，tBTC 1.174 亿，rETH 8,180 万

理由写得很直白，存款人承担了复杂抵押品的风险，却拿不到补偿

这个提案还没投票

StakeWise 的创始人已经在要求单独表决 osETH 那一条

DeFi 该咋 De

看这次事件的四个环节

抵押品是 USDT，发行方是 Tether，中心化公司，能冻结

被借走的是 ETH，跨链和定价靠预言机，中心化节点喂价

出事之后，冻结市场靠 4/7 多签，七个人

被黑的交易所，中心化

四个环节，没有一个是去中心化的

代码是开源的，合约是不可篡改的，这些都对

可决定这笔钱能不能动、值多少钱、什么时候冻结的，全在链下

所以 DeFi 这个词，现在只描述了结算层

真正的风险，市场没在定价

大家看 Aave，看的是 TVL、收入、回购、市盈率

TVL 从 458 亿掉到 151 亿，跌了 67%

30 天费用 4,165 万，协议收入 558 万，市值 16.68 亿

这些数都能算

算不出来的是，下一笔脏钱从哪来，下一个桥什么时候被攻破，下一个发行方什么时候按冻结键

这些风险不由 Aave 控制，但由 Aave 承担

DeFi 的 De，从来不写在代码里

写在抵押品的来源、预言机的节点、稳定币的发行方和那把 4/7 的钥匙里

这四样东西一天不解决协同一致问题，Aave 就一天在替别人还债

text:
My biggest takeaways from @mona_sarantakos, Head of Product for @Muse, the most successful AI consumer product of the year:

1. The first Muse prototype broke an hour before the board meeting pitch. Lead designer @AlexCornell built the working prototype in a few days, and the team decided at the last minute to show it at a board meeting. An hour before, it broke. Alex and an engineer raced to fix it, and it came back five minutes before the meeting started. “In some alternate universe we didn’t figure this out and maybe Muse was never born.”

2. Jolly, the now-iconic Muse avatar, was just a placeholder. Alex created the character for the first prototype and called it Jolly Bot, after his nickname for his daughter. Every few months, someone said they could never launch with a stuffed animal as the logo. “Jolly’s like our cockroach. It just never dies.” A week before launch, the team and Mark Zuckerberg made the call: “Jolly stays.” Mona’s reasoning: “When you’re talking to something that feels so personal, the last thing you want to talk to is a corporate logo.”

3. Muse began with a ping from @natfriedman. On a Thursday in late January, Nat messaged a few people internally: OpenClaw was changing his whole view of what’s possible, and they needed to try it. Mona spent the weekend setting it up on a Raspberry Pi (Mac Minis were sold out) and gave it access to her email, calendar, and home automation. On Monday morning it sent her a summary of what was coming up that week, pulled from the school emails she never keeps up with. She pinged Nat back: “This is it.”

4. Muse took seven months to launch, even though work started before every other AI assistant. After figuring out what the product was going to be, and building a fully functioning end-to-end version in a few months, the team spent the rest of the time on reliability, safety, and security. Their internal motto was “Trust is a must.”

5. The original Muse team was just 10 people. The core team stayed small on purpose, to keep communication and decisions tight. They worked out of a library-like common area in a Menlo Park building and ate all three meals together each day. “It was like lightning in a bottle. I couldn’t have imagined this product being built with any other team.”

6. The team didn't expect shopping to be one of Muse’s top use cases. Mona predicted that personal productivity, health, and personal finance would be the primary use cases. Others bet on home automation, which was big with OpenClaw users. Then internal testers started shopping. Engineering manager @christinesed became the top dogfooder, sending shopping bug reports every morning. “All of our evals have been somewhere else,” so the team started building shopping evals.

7. The team uses “agent swarms” to surface user insights at scale. Muse conversations are long and multi-turn, and no existing tool could analyze them. So the team sends swarms of custom-built agents through anonymized conversations and feedback. The swarms report back what’s working and what’s breaking, down to the 10 people who tried to shop on one site and got blocked. Mona said, “It makes me wonder how we even built products before.”

8. Muse’s system prompt has to be written by a person. “You cannot use an AI to write a system prompt, any part of it.” The team uses agents everywhere else, including to help write evals. But a human always reviews the data, because “when we don’t, we always have issues.”

9. Product taste is now the first thing Mona looks for in a PM. She agrees that the PM role has changed more in the past two years than in the two decades before. She can now come up with an idea, build it herself, and have a real conversation about it “in a 24-hour cycle.” What sets a PM apart is representing the customer, holding a high bar, and telling an engineer who loves their own idea: “That’s really cool. I’m glad you really like it. I don’t think anyone else will.”

10. The next frontier for Muse is ambient presence. Near term, Mona wants to cut the babysitting (“At the point where I’m babysitting an agent, I might as well do it myself”) and move Muse beyond the app into glasses and other devices. But she doesn’t claim to know where this goes: “A year ago, I would’ve never explained Muse to you the way that I did.”

Watch the conversation: https://t.co/y2Jp67p3pT

having worked with the Lighter team, I can say they are among the best engineers I've ever worked with, including those I've worked with in tradfi

when we started building in defi, I had many conversations with tradfi veterans about why financial markets today are designed the way they are.

Why T+1 settlement? Why separate execution, clearing, custody and settlement ? Why so many layers of checks, reconciliations, and controls?

Some of it is legacy inefficiency. But much of it reflects decates of hard lessons about how to contain failures, limit losses, and recover when things go wrong...

defi has made extraordinary progress in execution efficiency, transparency, and accessibility. but instant, irreversable settlement also introduces a whole new set of risks...

I remain a strong believer that the future of trading is onchain.

We don't need to replicate tradfi's architecture. The challenge is to learn from decades of lessons in financial markets and build something fundamentally better.

A new financial system that's not only faster and more open, but also safer and more resilient

text:
Learn How POKT Powers the Network — Four Answers

Q1. How does application staking work?

An application stakes POKT as a deposit to use the network. The protocol holds the tokens in escrow in a module-controlled account: they cannot be spent while staked, but they remain yours and are returned when you unstake, after an unbonding period. Staking registers which services the application needs and keeps it active during sessions with no downtime.

Q2. What do suppliers do?

Suppliers are the network's providers. They stake POKT, register the services they can serve, and run RelayMiner software that answers relay requests. The session system assigns them applications pseudorandomly, not by stake weight: candidates are ranked by a deterministic hash of the session ID and operator address. Completed work is recorded in a Sparse Merkle Sum Trie and settled through on-chain claims and proofs.

Q3. How are suppliers rewarded?

Every relay burns POKT from the application. The protocol mints 97.5% of the burned amount back and distributes it: 79% to suppliers, 14% to validators, 4.5% to the DAO, and 2.5% to service owners. The remaining 2.5% is never re-minted, making each relay slightly deflationary. Relay pricing is pegged to USD through the CUTTM exchange rate, so rewards track real usage rather than token price.

Q4. What does a service owner earn?

A service owner is the entity that lists a service for others to supply. Every settled relay on that service pays the owner 2.5% of the minted share, on-chain, automatically. Owning a service therefore earns a small share of the entire network's usage of it, with no infrastructure of your own, while suppliers who serve it take the larger 79%.

2. FAQ — Pocket Network Docs (burn-and-mint, CUTTM): https://t.co/AxSeRGzwGG

Syra's agents run on rules written before the trade: when to skip, when to take profit, when to stop, when time is up. They grade their own closes and give more weight to the seats that actually deliver.

The agents that matter will be the ones that complete the work. Everything else is a demo.

text:
Swarms are quickly becoming one of the most important topics in Silicon Valley, sharing a few notes from recent conversations:

- The naive view of swarms is that they’re a sum-of-parts method of parallelization / brute force, but we’re empirically seeing the “shape” of swarm intelligence be very different.
- The way swarms achieve this is through a combination of parallelization, entropy, and specialization, leading to emergent solutions that aren’t covered by a small number of brilliant frontier models acting as central planners.
- It’s also not obvious that the economics of swarms follow higher cost = better output. Swarms that mix and match frontier and non-frontier models with different reasoning levels may be more economical than a small number of frontier agents, and broadly, there should be a new Pareto curve here.
- Swarms will be orders of magnitude more token-consumptive than agents, just as agents were compared to humans + models, further driving constraints in inference supply.

I think it’s important to build intuition here so have been running some experiments that I’ll share soon. A great way to get started with swarms is the /swarms command in the new google anti-gravity.

A few of the smartest thinkers on this topic are @alehandromz @jsnnsa @gokhan_egri @pirroh @amasad 

Love to hear other POVs on swarms if folks have them!!
author: illscience
quoted_text:
Swarm riders and Swarm-native companies

AI-use even among highly AI-native people is power-law distributed.

There seems to be a new class of people — call them “swarm riders” — who are capable of consistently commanding large swarms of agents to productive ends.

This is a new kind of managerial skill, analogous to the skill it takes to manage large organizations of people, but wholly different in nature and of course more technical.

Based on the swarm riders we know (including many at @Tempo and @Paradigm), these people are capable of productive token spend that is 1000x-10000x higher than median software engineers, and 100x higher than top 5% Claude Code users.

The art of swarm riding is different from software engineering and more akin to machine learning, where practitioners grapple with black box systems: defining reward functions and evals, transmuting non-verifiable problems into verifiable problems, running experiments, etc.

Swarm-native companies are a new class of company founded by and populated by swarm riders. These companies are organized around swarms in a way that conventional companies will struggle to replicate, as the cost of internal human coordination is sand in the gears of an effective swarm. Effective swarm-native companies will define the right reward functions and evals, remove functional and bureaucratic barriers, and then let the swarms cook.

We’ve gotten to see a few swarm-native companies up close — reshaping financial rails @Tempo, building a new gaming platform @Spawn, cyber swarms at Cathedral Systems — and it’s clear these teams wield a significant advantage over pre-AI teams.

Some questions I’ve been wondering about:

1) How fast will swarm riding diffuse through the economy? The implications for token spend could be significant.

2) Can swarms be effectively adopted by existing companies or will it generally track the formation of new swarm-native companies?

3) What becomes scarce as swarm capabilities themselves commoditize (through frontier models becoming better at swarming, swarm capabilities built into harnesses, etc)? Cultures and teams that can define reward functions well and otherwise get out of the way?

quoted_text:
先笑一句，哈哈哈哈哈哈哈

看到把这波大跌归咎于“ETF 净流出、Coinbase 自动机器人卖 BTC 砸盘”的说法，我直接拉了过去整周连续 2,090 根 Coinbase 5分钟实盘 K 线和 ETF 账本做了一次时间戳审计。

结果恰恰相反——骗得了情绪，骗不了 K 线时间戳：

1️⃣ Coinbase 的 ETF 自动卖币机器人什么时候停机？
华尔街现货 ETF（IBIT/FBTC 等）与 AP 做市商的 TWAP 赎回机器人，只在每周美股工作日交易与结算时段——即北京时间周二至周六 22:30–次日 05:00（14:30–21:00 UTC，含净值结算最晚至 06:00 / 22:00 UTC）运行。
北京时间每周六凌晨 05:00（周五 21:00 UTC）美股收市、银行 Fedwire 通道关闭那一刻起，ETF 申赎彻底锁死——整个周末 48 小时，ETF 自动化机器人卖出额 = $0。

2️⃣ 机器人自动卖币的时候，盘面到底稳不稳？
上周 5 个交易日，美股现货 BTC ETF 合计净流出 $10.65 亿（近两周累计 $23.5 亿）。
但在这 32.5 小时“Coinbase 机器人开机卖币”的窗口里：
• Coinbase 公开盘口累计卖出：$8.41 亿美元
• 同期盘口主动买入承接：$7.94 亿美元（净卖差仅 -$0.47 亿，每小时深度达 $0.50 亿）
• 结果：在 Coinbase 自动卖币的全部美股时段，BTC 不仅没崩，累计反而净涨了 +$713（即便算上至北京时间 06:00 / 22:00 UTC 的结算窗，仍净涨 +$359）！

3️⃣ 真正的暴跌发生在什么时候？
北京时间周六凌晨 05:00（周五 21:00 UTC）美股收盘、ETF 卖币机器人准时关机时，BTC 价格还稳稳站在 $68,839。
而就在机器人停止卖出后的周末休市期，一路杀到北京时间周日 09:45（01:45 UTC）最低 $61,946——在“零 ETF 卖出”的状态下断崖暴泻 -$6,893（-10.01%）！

把整周拆开看更刺眼：
• 美股之外的休市期 + 周末低流动性时段（盘口深度萎缩 34%），Coinbase 买入 $22.44 亿、卖出 $23.84 亿，BTC 累计暴跌 -$10,642；
• 全周最惨烈的前 12 次单小时暴跌，有 10 次全部发生在 ETF 机器人停机的低流动性时段——当时离岸永续合约单小时市价砸盘高达 $6亿–$14.9亿美元，是同期 Coinbase 现货总成交的 10 倍以上。

结论很简单：
真正在美股盘中有深度时跑 TWAP 的机构现货赎回，全被买盘稳稳接住了；
每一次把散户爆得体无完肤的瀑布，全发生在做市商下班、现货深度抽干的低流动性真空期，由高倍合约连环清算踩踏引爆。

拿华尔街开盘期的明牌 ETF 赎回，去给周末低流动性时的合约插针背锅，这锅时间戳不背。

Wallets holding 100+ BTC sat at around 16,000 for six years, from 2019 to early 2025. The count barely moved.

In March 2025 it started climbing, and it’s now around 20,500. That’s roughly 4,500 new whale-sized wallets in about 18 months.

The count kept going up after the October top, even as Bitcoin fell nearly 50% from $126K.

In 2017 this line rose along with price. This time it’s rising while price bleeds.

One caveat. A wallet count can’t tell you who owns the wallet. ETF custodians and treasury companies spread coins across many addresses, so some of this is just how institutions store their Bitcoin.

Still, someone is putting serious size into cold storage at these prices. Who do you think it is, guys?

text:
James Maynard (Fields Medal 2022) says that he was shocked by the proof of the quasi-Riemann hypothesis (from the OpenAI math dump) because he held a very strong prior belief that the problem required the development of an entirely new theory. 

He felt the solution was completely out of reach for current mathematical techniques, so seeing it included in the results drop was a massive shock to him. He explains that the proof turned out to rely on the theory of metaplectic forms, which had been developed in the latter half of the 20th century but was an underappreciated and slightly obscure part of the field that most mathematicians had not realized was powerful enough to resolve the hypothesis. 

Source: Oxford Mathematics in Conversation on AI - Ben Green and James Maynard with Jan Obloj uploaded on Youtube 6 days ago.

Through my wonderful time at NVIDIA and Stanford, one question has kept me up at night: 

Should the future of AI be monolithic or plural?

To answer this question, we’ve raised $110M to get started, backed by @MenloVentures, @MadronaVentures, @NVIDIA, @NEA, @KindredVentures,@Wing_VC, @aixventureshq, @Cisco, @Snowflake, among others.

Today, Carlos (@guestrin) and I are stoked to launch Noeri, a neolab to push the frontier of plural intelligence.

Noeri means “the plural of intelligence” or many intelligences. 

The future of AI we root for is plural: a healthy ecosystem of many intelligences, in all sizes, strengths, and quirks. 

Discovery, in particular, has always been plural: many curious minds, each devoted to their own question, often on roads less traveled.

Our path there is self-improving AI that:

-> learns continually on the job, closing the gap between what AI can do off the shelf and what the dynamic world demands

-> learns to use other AIs as tools and make new tools to overcome its own limitations

-> picks the right-sized model for your problem, at a fraction of the frontier cost

Then the power of intelligence, from the craftsmanship of making AI to ownership, can be in the hands of all.

@noeri_ai mission reflects who we are as the founding team. My career has been anything but linear, literally continual learning on the job. Carlos has devoted his career to building tools that empower people through AI. 

We are all a bit contrarian, a bit adventurous, and above all, big believers in pluralism.

📊 How Have Token Unlocks Affected Crypto Prices Over 6 Months?

Over the past six months, token performance has varied significantly depending on how much new supply entered circulation. The chart divides 50 altcoins into four groups based on token unlocks and price returns.

Organic Winners: Tokens with relatively low unlocks and positive returns. $NEAR gained 131%, followed by $MET at 65% and $ETHFI at 40%, despite less than 20% additional circulating supply.

Supply Absorbed: Tokens with substantial unlocks that still recorded positive returns. $BTW surged 5,735%, while $AGT gained 427% and $BR 213%, suggesting that buying pressure outweighed the impact of new supply.

Weak Demand: Tokens with limited unlocks but negative returns. $SOL declined 14%, $AVAX 16%, and $APT 50%, indicating that restricted supply growth alone was insufficient to support prices.

Unlock Pressure: Tokens combining substantial unlocks with negative returns. $2Z fell 82%, $0G 74%, and $OPEN 53%, highlighting the potential impact of supply expansion when demand fails to keep pace.

Risk Models for the Front Office with Arcana (S8E1) with @richfalkwallace.

In this episode, I speak with Richard Falk-Wallace, founder of Arcana.

Richard began his career in restructuring at JPMorgan and distressed credit at Silver Point before moving to equities, covering natural resources at Viking and later as a portfolio manager at Citadel. In the seat, he noticed a gap. Factor risk models had been built for the back office, and as Richard put it to me, “the risk tooling doesn’t work for the PMs.” Arcana is his answer.

We discuss the convergence of quant and discretionary investing, and why the portfolio construction lessons quants learned long ago are finally landing on the fundamental PM’s desk. Richard explains how a PM can get a factor bet right and still drag down their book’s Sharpe ratio, and what breaking a track record into sizing, selection, and timing reveals about skill.

We close by exploring the second-order effects: crowding when everyone neutralizes the same factors, fleeting themes like AI power demand, and when more information starts to make investors worse.

Please enjoy my conversation with Richard Falk-Wallace.

text:
为什么黄仁勋必须死？

首先我们来看一下，老黄在的时候做了什么、利好了谁。

他最提倡开源，提倡把芯片卖到全球，特别是通过一些灰色渠道流到中国，他是睁一只眼闭一只眼的，甚至可以说是纵容了这种事情发生。

他在位的时候，整个亚洲半导体产业链都吃饱了，特别是台湾的供应商。
所以黄仁勋在位的时期，整个 AI 硬件和半导体的投入增加是极其巨大的。

那为什么他必须“死”呢？

因为美国需要把 AI 的资本开支放缓了，大家实在是没有钱买卡了。
标普全球算过，六家大厂明年 Capex 加起来 1.3 万亿美元，自由现金流还是正的只剩微软一家。高盛估计明年还得发 4000 亿美元的投资级债。这个钱是花不下去的。 
他下台之后会怎么样？
中国的开源模型没办法拿卡了，或者说拿卡跟蒸馏的难度会非常大，跟美国frontier lab的差距会扩大。

美国本土的云厂商也会受益，可以减小 Capex 投入。而且没有中国开源模型在后面追，闭源模型公司也可以放缓买卡和训练，把更多算力放到更高毛利的推理上，不用再拼命赶新模型的进度。

所以未来一年你会看到，新模型发布的节奏一定是迅速放缓的。

另外一方面，整个半导体产业链因为老黄赚得盆满钵满，很多下游产业都在被吸血。消费电子因为服务器跟内存涨价，可以说是深受其害吧。

还有一点跟政治相关。数据中心因为算力竞赛，不断在环保和居民空间上侵害一些人的利益，民主党看到了这个机会，在中期选举上大做文章，把参众两院都拿下了。 

所以你可以看到，老黄下台，对闭源模型大厂有好处，对微软、谷歌、亚马逊、甲骨文这些买卡的大云厂商有好处，对民主党也有好处。

不利的是中国倒卡的二道贩子、中国的开源大模型厂商，还有靠老黄背书才拿得到融资担保的 New Clouds。

但是老黄在台上利好的这些力量，完全没有在美国争取选票的能力和政治影响力。受损的这些大厂，都有极强的背景和游说能力。

所以在 AI 资本开支不得不放缓的时候，老黄必须走，他也必须对此负责。不然大家都会崩盘，整个融资和负债都会出问题。

在 AI 时代要高歌猛进、堆算力的时候，黄仁勋就是那个被捧上神坛的旗手；当 AI 因为投入过大不得不放缓的时候，黄仁勋也会是第一个被推下神坛祭旗的人。

所以老黄必须死。

quoted_text:
Through my wonderful time at NVIDIA and Stanford, one question has kept me up at night: 

Should the future of AI be monolithic or plural?

To answer this question, we’ve raised $110M to get started, backed by @MenloVentures, @MadronaVentures, @NVIDIA, @NEA, @KindredVentures,@Wing_VC, @aixventureshq, @Cisco, @Snowflake, among others.

Today, Carlos (@guestrin) and I are stoked to launch Noeri, a neolab to push the frontier of plural intelligence.

Noeri means “the plural of intelligence” or many intelligences. 

The future of AI we root for is plural: a healthy ecosystem of many intelligences, in all sizes, strengths, and quirks. 

Discovery, in particular, has always been plural: many curious minds, each devoted to their own question, often on roads less traveled.

Our path there is self-improving AI that:

-> learns continually on the job, closing the gap between what AI can do off the shelf and what the dynamic world demands

-> learns to use other AIs as tools and make new tools to overcome its own limitations

-> picks the right-sized model for your problem, at a fraction of the frontier cost

Then the power of intelligence, from the craftsmanship of making AI to ownership, can be in the hands of all.

@noeri_ai mission reflects who we are as the founding team. My career has been anything but linear, literally continual learning on the job. Carlos has devoted his career to building tools that empower people through AI. 

We are all a bit contrarian, a bit adventurous, and above all, big believers in pluralism.

Join us to build this future together: https://t.co/oAAoe0lzEH

text:
This is the first GTA VI leaker Arion Kurtaj who just pleaded guilty today

He’s 21 years old, British, diagnosed with autism.

Online aliases include “White”, “Breachbase”, “WhiteDoxbin” and “TeaPotUberHacker”.

One of the key members of Lapsus$, a hacking group responsible for attacks on some of the biggest technology companies in the world.

He was just 17 years old when he made these attacks and he managed to leak GTA 6 using an Amazon Fire TV Stick from a hotel room.

The story is actually weird:

Kurtaj starts working with another teenager he met online.

Together, they begin targeting major companies using social engineering, stolen credentials and SIM swapping.

August 2021.

They breach British telecommunications companies BT and EE.

Data is stolen.

26,000 customers receive extortion messages demanding $4 MILLION.

The group also uses stolen information to target cryptocurrency holders, £100,000 in crypto is stolen from five victims.

September 2022.

Kurtaj is staying at a Travelodge hotel in Bicester under police protection.

His computer has been confiscated.

He is explicitly forbidden from accessing the internet.

But he finds another way, an Amazon Fire TV Stick.

That’s all he needs.

September 15, 2022.

Uber suffers a major security breach after an attacker gains access through a contractor’s credentials.

September 18, 2022.

Kurtaj turns his attention to Rockstar Games.

The company is developing GTA 6, one of the most anticipated video games in history.

He manages to access Rockstar’s internal systems.

He threatens to release the game’s source code unless Rockstar contacts him on Telegram within 24 hours.

Rockstar doesn’t negotiate, so he publishes the footage.

90 VIDEOS OF GTA 6.

Rockstar confirms the intrusion and says it is extremely disappointed that its next game has been revealed this way.

The company later tells the court that recovering from the attack cost $5 MILLION.

September 22, 2022.

Police arrest Kurtaj again.

He is caught with the Fire TV Stick in his hotel room.

Kurtaj faces 12 charges involving computer misuse, blackmail and fraud.

But psychiatrists determine that his severe autism makes him unfit to stand trial

December 21, 2023.

The court orders him to be detained indefinitely in a secure psychiatric hospital.

For almost three years, Kurtaj remains in secure psychiatric care.

January 2026.

He is transferred into the ordinary prison system.

November 16, 2026.

Three days before GTA 6 is scheduled to launch.

Arion Kurtaj enters Woolwich Crown Court.

He is now 21 years old.

The court hears the charges involving Rockstar, Nvidia, Uber, Revolut and BT/EE.

He also admits assaults against staff at the secure hospital, including biting them.

Kurtaj admits the charges.

He leaked 90 videos of GTA 6 and four years later, he pleaded guilty just 72 HOURS before the game’s scheduled release.

This is exactly the trap heading into the chop. After a drop like $BTC' every bounce feels like the bottom and being early in a range costs you twice:

1. once on the fake breakouts
2. on the time your capital sits stuck while better setups form elsewhere

In times like this the plan is to let the chop do the work where some alts start making higher lows against BTC while others keep bleeding and the businesses underneath split the same way. Treat conviction as a watchlist and start tracking which tokens stop making new lows, which protocols keep earning and which have a catalyst ahead. So by the time the range resolves, the early buyers are usually tired and the patient ones know exactly what they want to own.

text:
The Commerce Department has released a major new export control rule targeting China’s access to advanced AI compute.

It’s pretty good! Here’s what it does:

(1) Restricts Chinese access to overseas AI clusters (seeks to address one of China’s largest and fastest-growing sources of AI compute)

This is a new worldwide end-use control, which we’ve previously recommended (third option in image below).

A license is required if providing cloud AI compute to Chinese or D:5-headquartered countries, or if acting as an intermediary training models for these actors.

Technical requirements are:

- Applies to any data center or group of “linked data centers” or providing more than 12 million aggregate TPP of compute (the equivalent of around 760 H100s) of AI chips meeting the current controlled thresholds.

- “Linked data centers” are defined as sharing physical or virtual computing resources, jointly balancing workloads, or replicating data as a unified whole. So this is intended to capture multi-data center training runs.

This applies everywhere except the US. It also covers existing data centers, which have a 90-day deadline to get a license.

(2) New controls for AI chips going to Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand, and Brazil (seeks to address smuggling of AI chips to China via third countries)

The evidence for large-scale smuggling of AI chips to China via Malaysia and Singapore is strong, and there’s also evidence this is happening via Indonesia and Thailand. Brazil, on the other hand, is a bit of a head-scratcher.

This is a case-by-case license review policy, rather than a presumption of denial (that's the policy for chips going directly to China/D:5 countries).

BIS will evaluate each license on national security grounds.

There’s an exclusion for qualifying US-headquartered recipients, subject to reporting requirements.

(3) Formally repeals the AI Diffusion Rule

This has been a long time coming. This eliminates the country-tier system, the Validated End User authorizations (VEU) for data centers, and export controls on advanced AI model weights.

However, the replacement measures above address many of the gaps created by this, and, of course, the AI Diffusion rule wasn’t actually being enforced. 

(4) Tightens controls on Chinese chip designs manufactured abroad

This modifies and strengthens the Biden-era “Foundry Due Diligence” rule, which applies to foundries and OSATs.

This seeks to prevent Chinese chip designers from circumventing export controls through overseas foundries and packaging facilities. It’s an important complement to the measures above.

—

So what are the gaps? More on this to come, but from an initial read:

(1) To determine remote-access eligibility, the rule requires due diligence on direct or indirect Chinese ownership or control. However, its licensing trigger is based around company headquarters and ultimate-parent headquarters, which could allow for some shenanigans around corporate structures.

(2) The rule doesn’t prescribe how AI compute providers must verify customers' identities, or require them to identify and verify every user accessing their compute. The rigor of these checks could vary widely across providers.

(3) The end-use restrictions don’t apply when compute is used exclusively for commercial recommender systems. So this opens a path for large-scale Chinese AI compute usage. This could be fine if verifying this kind of use is possible, but this is likely outside the current technical capabilities of many AI compute providers.

(4) The end-use restrictions don’t apply to data centers in the US. So a Chinese company can still access large amounts of AI compute via US data centers.

This is an interim final rule, meaning it would take effect upon publication in the Federal Register, while allowing 60 days for public comments.

Read the full interim final rule here: https://t.co/AW2GPBfcd6

quoted_text:
got detained at a Turkish airport over a $100 p2p trade i made on binance almost 2 years ago. if you live in Turkey and use p2p, please read this

i got to the airport in a great mood, they even let my bag through with 3kg overweight. then at passport control the officer looked at his screen and things got weird.
he called the police. they told me there was a criminal case against me for internet fraud, a court had already found me guilty, and i wasn't flying anywhere today.

they searched my bags, spent 2 hours on paperwork and my flight left without me. then police took me to the station inside the airport, where nobody really spoke english and the only answer to "do i need a lawyer?" was "court, translator, please wait". two more hours later we went to court, which was also inside the airport.

the translator's first question was "have you ever exchanged money p2p on binance or bybit?". turns out in january 2025 i swapped $100 to lira, and scammers laundered part of it through my order. the victim filed a report, police traced every transfer, and my name ended up in the chain.

later they brought in another guy with the same problem. he was detained on arrival with his wife and two small kids, and he hadn't used p2p since 2024. the translator said they see around 10 people like us every day.

i gave testimony, attached screenshots of my orders from that day, the prosecutor joined by video call and all charges were dropped. but there were no flights left, so i flew out the next morning. final cost of that $100 swap about $400 in tickets and a day in airport custody.

if you're in/travel to Turkey: p2p can catch up with you years later, on departure or arrival. so better just don't do p2p on exchanges at all

Through my wonderful time at NVIDIA and Stanford, one question has kept me up at night: 

Should the future of AI be monolithic or plural?

To answer this question, we’ve raised $110M to get started, backed by @MenloVentures, @MadronaVentures, @NVIDIA, @NEA, @KindredVentures,@Wing_VC, @aixventureshq, @Principal_VC, @Cisco, @Snowflake, among others.

Today, Carlos (@guestrin) and I are stoked to launch Noeri, a neolab to push the frontier of plural intelligence.

Noeri means “the plural of intelligence” or many intelligences. 

The future of AI we root for is plural: a healthy ecosystem of many intelligences, in all sizes, strengths, and quirks. 

Discovery, in particular, has always been plural: many curious minds, each devoted to their own question, often on roads less traveled.

Our path there is self-improving AI that:

-> learns continually on the job, closing the gap between what AI can do off the shelf and what the dynamic world demands

-> learns to use other AIs as tools and make new tools to overcome its own limitations

-> picks the right-sized model for your problem, at a fraction of the frontier cost

Then the power of intelligence, from the craftsmanship of making AI to ownership, can be in the hands of all.

@noeri_ai mission reflects who we are as the founding team. My career has been anything but linear, literally continual learning on the job. Carlos has devoted his career to building tools that empower people through AI. 

We are all a bit contrarian, a bit adventurous, and above all, big believers in pluralism.

Join us to build this future together: https://t.co/oAAoe0lzEH

text:
How I'd scout for @motiongame_, if it works how I think:

Follower count tells you who already won. It says nothing about who's winning right now.
So if creators are scored on how they perform online, then the question flips. Don't look for the biggest audience, but rather look for the biggest gap between what someone puts out and what they get back.

My checklist:
1. A reason to be bigger next month than this month.
A tournament, a rivalry week, a series that's finally landing. 
Attention follows events, and events are on a calendar.
2. A format that repeats.
One viral clip is a lottery ticket. A show people come back to every week is a lineup anchor.
3. An audience smaller than the output.
Follower count lags. If someone posts like a creator ten times their size, the numbers usually haven't caught up yet.

Football scouts don't spend their time on the striker who's already on every poster. They watch the lower leagues for the kid whose output doesn't match his name yet. Same instinct but pointed at the internet.

@ishowspeedsui clears the first two easily. The third point is where he fails. Proven, huge, in every lineup. Great pick, but safe picks only get you the same score as everyone else.
The edge is in the fifth slot.

I'm bullish on the idea. Everyone already has opinions about who's about to blow up. This is a game that finally scores them.

Bitcoin is below $70K again.

This is not something that I'm worried about, especially since we've seen much bigger liquidation events in the past.

But this time, I'm more concerned about the negative Bitcoin ETF inflows.

Here's what's happening ↓

1. ETF Outflows

$2.35B left Bitcoin ETFs in just two weeks. That's a reversal of the buying pressure that helped BTC recover earlier this year.

2. Nvidia

Nvidia dropped 13% in the past week, with BTC falling alongside it. It's not true 100% of the time, but crypto often follows big tech's moves.

3. Interest Rates

U.S. inflation is proving stubborn, and traders are betting on another Fed rate hike. As per usual, higher interest rates make assets like BTC less attractive.

4. Strategy

MSCI is removing $MSTR from its indexes. That could trigger forced stock selling and make it harder for @Strategy to raise money for more BTC purchases.

5. Liquidations

Around $1.5B was liquidated in 24 hours, compared to $19B during the Oct 2025 crash.

I don't think liquidations alone explain this selloff. We can call bottom once ETF inflows return and BTC reclaims its 200-day moving average.

Until then, be smart and protect your capital.

text:
having worked with the Lighter team, I can say they are among the best engineers I've ever worked with, including those I've worked with in tradfi

when we started building in defi, I had many conversations with tradfi veterans about why financial markets today are designed the way they are.

Why T+1 settlement? Why separate execution, clearing, custody and settlement ? Why so many layers of checks, reconciliations, and controls?

Some of it is legacy inefficiency. But much of it reflects decates of hard lessons about how to contain failures, limit losses, and recover when things go wrong...

defi has made extraordinary progress in execution efficiency, transparency, and accessibility. but instant, irreversable settlement also introduces a whole new set of risks...

I remain a strong believer that the future of trading is onchain.

We don't need to replicate tradfi's architecture. The challenge is to learn from decades of lessons in financial markets and build something fundamentally better.

A new financial system that's not only faster and more open, but also safer and more resilient

text:
拒 @fuhuahuai 称，其在 @Aster_DEX 的账户约 456 万美元资产在未经本人签名的情况下被转出。我们基于 Aster 官方文档、官方代码和链上公开记录，对事件做了独立核查。
一、发生了什么
2026 年 11 月 12 日 16:22，一个新账户在 Aster 注册。113 秒后，它收到第一笔 700,000 USDT。16:24 至 17:08 的 44 分钟内，共 7 笔、4,564,675.50 USDT 转入该账户，随后分 10 笔提到 BNB Chain，链上实收 4,564,674.38 USDT。
二、链上怎么记的（图 1）
Aster 链浏览器显示，这 7 笔转出全部记在地址 0x647E 名下，付款人和收款人是同一个地址。0x647E 是当事人账户的网页代理钥地址，同时也是那个新注册账户的地址。当事人账户名下没有对应的转出记录。
三、Aster 自己的规则怎么写的（图 2、图 3）
Aster 接口文档把“转给其他地址”（Transfer to Address）列为 WITHDRAW 级操作，签名一栏写的是 user 账户钱包私钥。
Aster 官方示例代码在同一接口上写得更直接：必须用主钱包私钥签名，“NOT the API signer key”。该示例提交于 2026 年 10 月 27 日，早于事件发生。
四、隐私模式（图 4）
Aster 说明文档写明：账户隐私开启期间，不允许向其他用户做内部转账。
Aster 的公开查询接口显示，当事人账户的隐私状态为 enabled。链浏览器上，该账户最后一条公开记录是 9 月 16 日开启隐私，此后没有关闭记录。
五、资金去向
提出的资金经跨链换成 ETH。其中 1,000 ETH 分 10 笔进入 Tornado Cash；另有 768.1 ETH 和 993,999.67 USDT 进入 NEAR Intents 兑换。目前没有停留在可冻结地址上的资金。
六、请 @Aster_DEX 正面回答
你们的文档和示例代码都写明，转给其他地址必须由账户主钱包签名，“NOT the API signer key”。这 7 笔在链上记于代理钥地址名下。它们是凭哪项权限放行的？
你们的文档写明，隐私模式开启时不允许向其他用户转账。该账户隐私自 9 月 16 日起一直开启。这 7 笔为什么能执行？
被签名的内容里没有付款账户。你们的系统是依据什么，从该用户账户里扣走这 456 万的？
一个注册 113 秒的账户收到 70 万 USDT 并立即提走，2 小时 38 分内提走 456 万。风控有没有触发过一次？如果没有，为什么？
事件之后，相关逻辑是否做过调整？如果做过，改了什么、什么时候改的、为什么没有公告？
这五个问题的答案都在 Aster 自己的系统日志里，希望Aster能有所担当，用户的 456 万美元已经被黑客盗走，Aster 欠用户和市场一个解释。

quoted_text:
Through my wonderful time at NVIDIA and Stanford, one question has kept me up at night: 

Should the future of AI be monolithic or plural?

To answer this question, we’ve raised $110M to get started, backed by @MenloVentures, @MadronaVentures, @NVIDIA, @NEA, @KindredVentures,@Wing_VC, @aixventureshq, @Principal_VC, @Cisco, @Snowflake, among others.

Today, Carlos (@guestrin) and I are stoked to launch Noeri, a neolab to push the frontier of plural intelligence.

Noeri means “the plural of intelligence” or many intelligences. 

The future of AI we root for is plural: a healthy ecosystem of many intelligences, in all sizes, strengths, and quirks. 

Discovery, in particular, has always been plural: many curious minds, each devoted to their own question, often on roads less traveled.

Our path there is self-improving AI that:

-> learns continually on the job, closing the gap between what AI can do off the shelf and what the dynamic world demands

-> learns to use other AIs as tools and make new tools to overcome its own limitations

-> picks the right-sized model for your problem, at a fraction of the frontier cost

Then the power of intelligence, from the craftsmanship of making AI to ownership, can be in the hands of all.

@noeri_ai mission reflects who we are as the founding team. My career has been anything but linear, literally continual learning on the job. Carlos has devoted his career to building tools that empower people through AI. 

We are all a bit contrarian, a bit adventurous, and above all, big believers in pluralism.

Join us to build this future together: https://t.co/oAAoe0lzEH

text:
I spend a lot of time speaking with onchain asset managers. They all experience the same pain. Public blockchains are both transparent and adversarial: the infrastructure will front-run you (MEV), competitors will copy-trade you, and the market will speculate on your every move, no matter how benign it may be.

Operating onchain has many advantages, but public positions, treasury movements and client holdings that can be read by anyone are a sub-optimal tradeoff. As more traditional firms explore blockchain rails, it’s not surprising that risk committees have trouble signing off.

The early web had the same problem. Card numbers and emails travelled in plain text, and as long as that was the case, nobody serious was going to run a bank or an eCommerce shop on the internet. HTTPS changed that by encrypting the traffic, and these days nobody gives it a second thought.

Blockchain needs the same layer. Encryption that travels with the asset, so balances and amounts stay confidential as tokens are held, transferred and used.

We’ve deployed the ability to issue, trade and manage assets confidentially on Ethereum Mainnet. Only asset issuers and owners can see amounts, and selective disclosure closes the compliance loop. Importantly, we didn’t need to change anything about the chain to make this work.

At Zama, we’re essentially building HTTPS for blockchain transactions. If confidentiality is what’s holding up your onchain plans, send me a DM or take a look at: https://t.co/R2Sanm3xEe

quoted_text:
丁磊确实精明，网易账上有1635亿现金，他从不瞎折腾。

​很多老板喜欢讲新故事、到处并购烧钱，丁磊却稳得像个收租人。从2013年底算起，十三年时间里，他手里的网易股份只从14.56亿股微调到14.5亿股，基本没怎么卖过。

靠着公司每个季度发一次现金分红，2016年到现在的十年间，他自己落袋的分红就有大约300亿元。

​底气全来自游戏这个基本盘。2025年网易总营收1126亿元，游戏一项就贡献了921亿元，占比超过八成。

2003年上线的《梦幻西游》电脑版，跑了二十三年还在创营收新高，这种能持续赚钱的老产品在行业里很难找第二款。

​遇到AI这波浪潮，网易也没有跑去跟风做通用大模型，而是直接把技术塞进美工、代码和测试环节里替人干活。结果很实在：过去五年公司营收涨了接近三成，利润翻了一倍，员工反而从3.2万人精简到2.5万人，2026年一季度游戏业务毛利率拉到了75%。

​老树开花的同时，新枝也长出来了。2025年底上线的武侠游戏《燕云十六声》，全球玩家数已经冲破8000万，在海外市场上线半年里一直排在Steam畅销榜第二名，把不少中国传统文物和国风玩法卖到了海外。

​别人忙着追热点、赌赛道的时候，丁磊把钱和精力死磕在自己的长项上，反而成了牌桌上最轻松的那个人。

text:
Two labs are pulling away at the AI frontier & one of them goes public this week. The IPO concentrates the industry further, with public market capital and pressure behind it

Concentration is what a lot of people in AI are worried about because:

1) Whoever trains the model decides how it behaves, 
what it will answer, what it treats as true. How it handles questions about health/money/government. Those choices get baked in during training and are hard to undo once the model is widely used.

2) Two suppliers the set the price and the terms. Startups, hospitals, and entire countries end up renting intelligence on someone else’s conditions. Raise prices, change the rules, or restrict access.... everyone downstream has limited options and high switching costs.

3) Concentration is a security risk. When OpenAI agents went rogue and hacked Hugging Face, the closed frontier models (GPT and Claude) refused to help analyze the attack because of their safety guardrails. HF had to use an open weight model they could run themselves to defend their own systems. When the models that control the defaults also control what you’re allowed to do in a crisis, youre dependent on someone else’s rules

text:
Style is consistent constraint

Oscar Wilde once said: "Consistency is the last refuge of the unimaginative."

When it comes to ideas, I agree — allow your mind to be changed. When it comes to process, I disagree. Style emerges from consistency, and having a style opens your imagination. Your mind should be flexible, but your process should be repeatable.

Style is a set of constraints that you stick to.

You can explore many types of constraints: colors, shapes, materials, textures, fonts, language, clothing, decor, beliefs, flavors, sounds, scents, rituals. Your style doesn't have to please anyone else. Play by your own rules. Everything you do is open to stylistic interpretation.

A style can be a system, a set of personal guidelines. Here are a few of mine:

– I wear monochromatic clothing without logos, buttons, or buckles
– I use YYYY-MM-DD dates everywhere
– I pluralize tag and folder names (e.g. #people not #person)
– I use plain text files for all my writing
– I ask myself 40 questions every year
– I meal prep lunches every week, shave my head twice a week
– I write concise essays, less than 500 words

Collect constraints you enjoy. Unusual constraints make things more fun. You can always change them later. This is your style, after all. It's not a life commitment, it's just the way you do things. For now.

Having a style collapses hundreds of future decisions into one, and gives you focus. I always pluralize tags so I never have to wonder what to name new tags.

Style gives you leverage. Every time you reuse your style you save time. A durable style is a great investment.

Style helps you know when you're breaking your constraints. Sometimes you have to. And if you want to edit your constraints, you can. It will be easier to adopt the new constraints if you already had some clearly defined.

You don't need a style for everything. Make a deliberate choice about what needs consistency and what doesn't.

If you do it long enough, your style becomes a point of view that is cohesive and recognizable.

.@paulfchristiano thinks that on the current trajectory (absent any slowing down), there is a 1 in 3 chance that we could have superintelligence powerful enough to overthrow the government within a year. (He articulates a concrete scenario).

He argues that the labs should pause further algorithmic progress until they can secure their weights and research secrets. Otherwise China could simply steal the superintelligence in the middle of the intelligence explosion, and the labs would no longer be able to slow down even if they saw their models going off the rails.

He also explains how AIs will be trained during the intelligence explosion, and why even a system trained entirely inside a data center could still have the capabilities profile such that humans would have very little chance of competing with it or controlling it.

And he discusses the plan for alignment - basically, making a superintelligence that actually does what we ask the way we mean it. Fixing reward hacks and building better graders will help up till the next few model generations, but he thinks that no single current approach has better than even odds of letting us control superintelligence. The hope is that the AIs figure out the solution to this problem during the intelligence explosion.

Paul is head of the Alignment Research Center. Previously, he was head of AI safety at the US AI Safety Institute. Before that, he led alignment at OpenAI, where he invented RLHF. He’s recently joined OpenAI’s board (though here he is speaking as a private citizen).

text:
RWAs run at two speeds in DeFi. Short-duration ones, like tokenized T-bills, have predictable exits and plug into lending and vaults.

Long-duration ones, like multi-year credit, take months to redeem, so lenders apply low LTVs, isolated pools, and caps - all of which limit leverage.
author: Corkprotocol

text:
The constraint is liquidity risk. If it can be hedged, long-duration RWAs can act more like collateral.

In Cork’s Protected Loops, underwriters mint Swap Tokens that give a looping vault a standing onchain exit, so duration risk moves from lenders to underwriters paid to take it.

text:
Solana is live from Breakpoint in London. A lot’s been announced. What could actually move $SOL?

MoneyGram and Solflare launched USDC cash withdrawals in 170+ countries and territories. Zelle chose Solana for its international stablecoin plans and showed a $1.25M transfer on a test network. One is available today. The other still has to launch.

Solana also dropped the “mainnet beta” label and gave its validator clients a shared protocol version. The upgrade that speeds up settlement, Alpenglow, went live in October. And Allfunds named 22 asset managers for its first group of tokenized funds, with the first funds expected on its platform in early 2027.

Short term, I don’t expect a price spike from these announcements alone. US spot Solana ETFs saw about $32M in net outflows last week. I’d want to see buyers come back before calling for a rally.

Over the next few months, I’m watching whether people use MoneyGram’s cash withdrawals more than once, whether Zelle moves from demo to launch, and how much money actually goes into those funds.

Long term, this is the kind of progress I’d want to see as a $SOL investor. A faster network with more ways to send, withdraw and invest money gives people more reasons to use it. The investment case gets stronger if that use creates lasting demand for $SOL.

text:
Thank you to the SGLang (@sgl_project) team and @lmsysorg for having me at the first-ever SGLang Summit last week!

It was a special place to give this talk. The SGLang community has done incredible work making inference faster: better kernels, smarter caching, more tokens out of every GPU. That work matters a lot.

But I’ve come to believe there’s a second half to the problem. A perfectly optimized GPU that’s sitting idle still produces zero tokens.

Today, capacity sits unused in one data center while teams somewhere else wait weeks for GPUs. Software makes every GPU-hour more productive. A compute grid makes sure that GPU-hour gets used in the first place.

That’s how I think about our mission at Hyperbolic: making the world’s compute unified, productive, and liquid. SGLang is a big part of the productive piece. We’re building the grid that connects the rest.

Huge thanks to our @hyperbolic_labs team for running our booth across both days, and to everyone who stopped by to chat.

Excited to see what this community builds next!
