quoted_text:
My memo to our clients this morning:

Yesterday, we doubled our already profitable S&P 500 short exposure because we believe the potential for further downside remains worth the miniscule risk we are taking. Our original position has been completely de-risked, and the additional shares were added using what we call an "add and reduce" technique", allowing us to increase exposure without materially increasing overall risk. This puts us in our favorite position: large profit potential with very small risk.

The Nasdaq triggered a follow-through day. We take that seriously, but now we need to see whether the rally can gain traction or if distribution rears its head in the coming days. With a good-sized hedge bet in place, we are open to adding some longs as they meet our criteria. Currently, the list is small, but there are a few names we are considering. Refer to our Focus List for current names.

Many of yesterday's biggest winners were in the AI/technology stocks that had been beaten down and severely oversold. CoreWeave is an especially good illustration. It exploded 24.7% yesterday, but closed at $60.77 versus a 52-week high of $138.2 - still down about 56% below its high. IREN gained 5.6% but closed at $20.84 against a $70.71 high, still roughly 71% below its high. Those are enormous rallies but occurring inside badly damaged charts. Most of yesterday's tech stock rallies occurred within strong downtrends.

Macro and policy risks still argue for staying selective rather than chasing a market with very few sound stock setups. Sticky inflation, the prospect of additional Fed rate hikes, rising long-term interest rates, and increasing talk of regulation surrounding AI and data centers are all reasons to remain cautious about a nascent rally that, so far, has largely been a rebound from an oversold condition.

Interest rates remain particularly important. After pulling back from an overbought condition, the 10-year yield has started turning higher again, while the 1-year yield jumped sharply. That is not exactly the backdrop you want to see if you’re looking for expanding equity valuations and a sustained risk-on move.

Investors Intelligence bulls fell sharply to 37.0% from 42.6% last week, the lowest bullish reading since early April, when bulls reached 33.3%. That's a significant reversal from just six weeks ago, when bulls stood at 57.7% as the S&P 500 and Nasdaq were hitting highs. That peak was one of three readings above the 55% danger level that historically signals elevated risk.

At the same time, bears jumped to 24.1% from 18.5%, the highest bearish reading since April. The shift is encouraging from a contrary-sentiment standpoint, particularly after several weeks when bearish readings remained unusually low.

Sentiment is definitely moving in the right direction, but we don't believe the ratio of bulls to bears has reached the extreme normally associated with a major contrary buy signal. For now, we view the change primarily as a directional indication. Optimism is being wrung out and pessimism is building as stocks retreat from their highs. That's constructive, but it isn't necessarily capitulation. We would like to see sentiment deteriorate further before treating it as a powerful contrary signal.

A follow-through day is important piece of evidence, but it is not a license to blindly rush back into the market. The real confirmation will come from the market of stocks - better price action, expanding leadership and a proliferation of quality setups emerging from sound bases.

For now, we are taking a measured approach. We will look to add some long exposure incrementally as individual stocks prove themselves. We strongly advise you only get aggressive on the heels of portfolio traction. The weight of evidence suggests that we are not yet completely out of the woods. Let the market earn your exposure. For now, maintain short (hedge) exposure and adhere to stops.

text:
Lighter admitted their vulnerability, but the way more interesting part is how the api key got stolen from Abraxas

no access to hardware, their servers, accounts or anything else. just public data and a bit of math

every order on Lighter is signed with an API key. the signature is public (well, not anymore), the key is secret

to keep the key from being calculated, every signature gets a random one-time number mixed in. it's called a nonce

simplified:
signature = nonce + hash × key
hash = fingerprint of the tx, everyone can see it

as long as the nonce is fresh every time, there's no way to get the key. two unknowns, one equation

the trader's bot was signing with its own homemade code instead of the official lighter sdk. and used the same nonce twice

say key = 7, nonce = 10
tx 1, hash 3: 10 + 3×7 = 31
tx 2, hash 5: 10 + 5×7 = 45

the hacker subtracts: 45 − 31 = (5 − 3) × key
14 = 2 × key
key = 7

irl the numbers are ~100 digits long, but the math is the same.

and you know the rest..

Prosecutors said they lured crypto trading bots into a trap with a trade that "looked like one thing from the outside, but was secretly something else."

text:
Google DeepMind's Alex Imas says AI agents still struggle to coordinate, and that's a key bottleneck to economic transformation:

"What you actually need for real economic transformation is not just competence... It's the ability of these agents to coordinate with one another."

"There's this idea of agentic swarms, right? But if you unpack it, these agents are still very bad at coordinating. They're not coordinating, they're mostly just doing parallel processing."

"If you have benchmarks specifically on coordination, you could actually show that 1 agent does better than 2 agents splitting the work, even if they can communicate. Whereas if you give the same thing to people, they actually have division of labor, they communicate, and they do way better than 1 person with double the resources."

"But if they get better at coordinating, you can basically break the Coasean ceiling on firm size, and you can get very, very different firms to emerge."

"Once coordination becomes better, the economic space of possibilities of what firms look like, what happens to wages, what happens to employment, that's when the real kind of visible changes are going to happen."

text:
Well, most of the time projections are noise and reactionary. 

Like right now, sky-high projections for $ANT $700-$800B ARR over next few years is stirring up hype that I'd argue gets revised down later. 

I do think it's important to model in capex forecasts dropping past 2028, due to the current reflexive nature of AI selloffs, rate hikes, etc. 

The drawn out duration of Iran War doesn't help, Jensen leaving $NVDA certainty draws concerns over Nvidia's ecosystem. 

But any catalyst, like if Iran War ends, can also change sentiment in a heartbeat (since bearish positioning is overwhelming). 

- It's also clear financing has been tightening, since OpenAI only managed to raise $11B of their original $30B target so far. 

- Markets are reacting enthusiastically to companies like $TE doing a $100M ATM today (nuking valuations)

- Although the "guppy" sector is probably the most sensitive to financing + rate changes.

On bright side... Neoclouds like $NBIS or $IREN  seem to be adjusting by getting 100% capex prepayments or 90% GPU prepayments from their counterparties. 

What I'd argue though is lower aggregate capex does not apply uniformly in supply chains.

- Mid-high range lasers for NPO/CPO are still sold out, as seen with $LITE now starting negotiations for 2030 capacity.  
- MLCCs are seeing further tightening as content usage goes up for AI servers
- ABF substrates to InP substrates not really going anywhere. 

If content per system goes up 10X-15X, capacity expands at 2-3X Y/Y, and capex drops 28%. 

And content is so cheap that you can triple order and screw over competitors with wafer supply... 

I'm pretty confident you'll see acceleration upstream in bottlenecks from optical components to substrates despite potential aggregate capex dropping. 

Another rant is: 

-I keep seeing this argument that "low P/E is a warning for cyclical that's going to crash" but these are just clown takes

Nobody seems to analyze duration scenarios like capacity expansion vs. content changes vs. demand. to actually see how long those earnings last. 

If everyone seems to be exiting DDR2 lines, there's probably going be more tightness in 2027 despite consume demand weakening, even if it looks like it's low P/E. 

- Also for concerns about CPO "delays", the same components like lasers are used for NPO. You'll still see 150-200mW NPO lasers or ELS NPO using the same 300–400+ mW lasers as CPO. 

We'll just see acceleration with NPO as a bridge if CPO gets delayed and higher range lasers likely to remain in a severe shortage. 

- Feels like markets have also completely discredited the merit of take/pay price floor LTAs as well that companies like SK Hynix to Samsung have.

If contractual agreements hold up, memory players look very undervalued.  

TLDR:
- I think it's important to model in capex decreasing to numbers like -30% in hypothetical downside sceanrios. 

Given AI profitability, it's clearly not sustainable for hyperscalers to aggregately increase capex $500B or $1T+ Y/Y, and that's never been a case I've argued. 

- This is also not the same thing as demand destruction that markets are overreacting to now (which haven't happened yet). 

- We can see demand revisions for GPUs, ASICs, and heavier cost parts of the supply chain, while acceleration increases elsewhere.  

The nuances market miss by indiscriminately selling everything is going to present compelling opportunities when the dust settles. I think in the end institutions are probably going to end up owning more of the same names retail discovered early on. 

Anyway, I think it's a good idea to try and survive until more earnings comes out.

text:
细节出来了，比上周日纽时那版草案狠得多。

商务部这次发的是临时最终规则，编号RIN 0694-AK50，四块内容，每一块都在堵路。

第一块，全球兜底。 向全世界任何一家数据中心出口AI芯片和服务器，只要它可能向中国、澳门或D:5集团（中国、俄罗斯、伊朗、朝鲜等22国）的公司提供超过1200万TPP的算力，就要申请许可。1200万TPP大概相当于750颗H100/H200。已经在提供这类服务的运营商，规则生效后90天内必须拿到许可。

翻译一下，以前是管芯片运到哪，现在管算力从哪调。你在东南亚、中东、甚至欧洲的数据中心，只要远程给中国公司提供超过那个门槛的算力，就算出口，就得拿许可。

第二块，五国点名。 向新加坡、马来西亚、印尼、泰国、巴西出口最先进芯片，从H100起，也要许可，理由是高于正常水平的转运风险。例外是芯片最终给在当地运营的美国公司用。新加坡在名单上，就在它刚签了美国主导的Pax Silica宣言的那个周末。宣言签完，芯片还是得拿许可，这个画面本身就挺说明问题。

第三块，拜登那套AI扩散规则正式废了。 2025年1月那套国家分级、模型权重管制、数据中心VEU计划全部取消，BIS自己说它从未执行过。废掉旧框架，换上来的是一套更直接、更宽的全球兜底加五国点名。

第四块，不管什么。 电商和社交媒体的商业推荐系统不在内。

上周日纽时那版草案说的是卢特尼克推的收窄版，7个国家，只管未来出货，报备就行。正式规则口径更广，全球数据中心兜底加五国点名，而且要的是许可，不是报备。

这跟之前Megaspeed那条线是直接接上的。

Megaspeed在马来西亚的机房，Aperia在新加坡的通道，这些之前给中国企业提供远程算力的灰色路径，靠的就是租算力不算出口这个定义缝隙。今天这个缝隙被正式焊死了。新加坡和马来西亚这两个案子里最关键的中转国，现在买最先进芯片本身就要许可，远程租算力也要许可。两头都上了锁。

所以英伟达在东南亚的生意，逻辑变了。以前东南亚数据中心是英伟达芯片流向中国的一条变相出口通道，现在这条通道在规则层面走不通了。英伟达要么失去这部分变相需求，要么承担合规成本去证明每一颗芯片最终没有被中国公司远程用到。无论哪种，东南亚的增量故事都得重新算。

明天财报电话会上，Kress对远程租赁和东南亚客户怎么描述，会直接撞上这条新规。芯片不让卖、算力不让租之后，英伟达在东南亚的生意还怎么做，这个临时ceo的回答很重要。

author: Kshsb783142
quoted_text:
美国商务部今天正式发布新规，把AI芯片的出口管制从“管实物”正式延伸到了“管访问”。以前是芯片运到中国才管，现在你在新加坡、马来西亚的数据中心，远程调用英伟达的算力来训练模型，一样要被管起来。

先把规则本身说清楚。

这7个国家被正式纳入管制清单：新加坡、马来西亚、泰国、印尼、巴西、挪威、南非。从今天起，这些国家进口英伟达Blackwell及以上级别的芯片，必须向BIS申请许可，披露芯片最终给谁用、用来干什么，并接受持续监控。

但真正被堵死的，是“远程访问”这条路。 以前中国企业把芯片买不到，就去东南亚租一个机柜，远程调用算力来训练模型。芯片不跨境，许可审查够不着。新规把这个口子封上了：只要你是受美国武器禁运的国家（中国、俄罗斯等），就不能远程访问这些数据中心里的先进算力。

美资数据中心有一个“豁免”，但代价很清楚。 美国公司在上述7国运营的数据中心，如果能确保中国、俄罗斯等受限国家无法远程接入，可以免于申请芯片进口许可。但必须向BIS报告客户身份和算力规模。说白了，你可以继续做生意，但不能再装傻，客户是谁得说清楚。

为什么是现在出，这件事比规则本身更值得琢磨。

韩国联合通讯社在报道里点了一句很关键的话：这项新规，是英伟达过去一直通过游说反对的政策。现在它被推进下去，反映的是黄仁勋丑闻之后，英伟达在华盛顿的政治影响力正在减弱。

换句话说，如果黄仁勋还在，这条规则未必会在这个时间点、以这个力度落地。 老黄过去几年一直在推对华芯片销售，跟白宫关系走得近，是挡在出口管制前面的一道阻力。他走了，阻力没了，规则就来了。之前聊过，干掉黄仁勋的不是婚外情，是那个需要他倒下的政策窗口。今天这条规则，就是那个窗口里落下来的东西。

对我们关心的AI算力链意味着什么。

短期看，东南亚的数据中心运营商首当其冲。Megaspeed在马来西亚的机房、Aperia在新加坡的通道，这些之前给中国企业提供远程算力的灰色通道，从今天起在规则层面走不通了。需求会寻找新的出口，但短期内的摩擦成本是实打实的。

对英伟达来说，这件事的信号很拧巴。它的芯片依然是这条链上最值钱的东西，但它的政治靠山已经倒了。新规落地之后，英伟达在华盛顿的话语权只会进一步收缩，以后每一条出口管制规则出来，它都很难再像以前那样挡在前面。

从管芯片，到管算力，再到管远程访问。华盛顿在一步一步地把“中国拿到先进算力”的每一条路都堵上。而英伟达失去的那个人，恰好是过去几年在这些规则面前唯一能说上话的人。

Crowley's role in the orgies, which has not been previously reported, highlights the nexus between the world of AI research and the lurid subcultures of Silicon Valley, where the people shaping the behavior of powerful AI systems often behave in obscene and offensive ways. Red Means No was cofounded by Aella, a Bay Area escort whose partner, Nate Soars, is the president of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI), an influential AI safety group in Berkeley, Calif. Aella started the kink parties, she wrote in a 2023 post, after she "attended a vanilla orgy" and found herself "wishing someone would just come over and take me despite my complete lack of enthusiasm."

While it's hard to know what percentage of attendees work in AI, Red Means No's business records suggest that the overlap is substantial. In addition to Crowley, who joined Anthropic last year, the LLC’s 2023 filing listed two other AI researchers as managers: Aaron Silverbrook, the former director of operations at MIRI, and Rosie Campbell, the managing director of Eleos AI, a nonprofit that researches the "potential well-being and moral patienthood of AI systems."

Silverbrook has stated that he runs "Aella's media empire" and describes himself as a "reasonable doomboy concerned about being paperclipped in an AI apocalypse before 2030." Campbell, who is no longer listed as manager of Red Means No, worked on OpenAI's safety team before joining Eleos, where she conducted a "model welfare" evaluation of Anthropic's Claude 4 model. She was also advertised as a featured guest at an AI safety meet-up organized by Aella, who this year hosted a "bootcamp" for influencers concerned about "AI doom."

The application for the bootcamp, "Plz Don't Kill Us," included the following question: "If you had to have sex with a cow would you rather it be dead or alive?"

Privacy for everyone. Zcash for everyone.

text:
HOGE was a great call. No manual boosts, every payout comes from the same scorer. Rewards aren't set per callout or by the multiple. Each day we score the caller, then split that across their calls by tail volume. LS had about $10.3k of tail volume, HOGE about $7.1k.

As Alon covered in his last post, each day is a fresh pot shared across every caller. Your score doesn't map to a dollar amount, it sets your share of that day's pot relative to everyone else scored that day, so similar calls can pay differently day to day.

The Degen pot rewards active callers, but your score reads how your calls land on average over 7 days, not just your best one. You had 96 live calls in that window vs schoen's 15, so HOGE got averaged in with a lot of noise: about $154 tail volume per call vs $934.

这轮 AI 行情的结构性裂缝，早在 INTC 财报爆雷时就已经暴露了。

产业链盈利分化、增长预期透支、资本开支与实际回报不匹配，问题从来不是某一个人的去留。

老黄的新闻，不过是压垮市场情绪的最后一根稻草，而不是一切问题的起因。

是散户的大脑内存被覆盖了，还是脑子里的缓存从来就没装过基本面？究竟是AI最缺存储还是我们人类自己的记忆？

I know everyone wants to blame some whale, Binance, the Anthropic IPO, or a sudden change in BTC's long-term outlook for the recent weakness. 

But these explanations only tell us about the emotional state of the person making the claim. 

They tell us nothing about what actually transpired. 

What I think actually happened is BTC miners started selling again into a fairly weak tape in late October (you can see in the chart that miner selling started each correction in '26 that led to a capitulation). 

And I think part of the reason the tape was so weak is that the market was convinced we had entered the "early bull" (myself included) after the technical confirmation in September. 

So, lots of money had already entered the market. And there just wasn't enough dry powder to buy up what the miners were selling. 

Of course, this then led to every leveraged position since August getting liquidated. 

The same folks I referred to as "the least volatile" at any point in the cycle a few weeks back proved to be quite emotional and volatile as soon as the price moved lower (at least the new money that came in; we see no evidence of long-term holders in profit selling). 

----

If you don't have good data and a sound strategy to fall back on, it's easy to let the market's emotions get to you.

text:
This podcast really got me thinking. There's been a lot of worry about superintelligent AIs "overthrowing the government."

I think this is the wrong picture of how superintelligent AIs will behave. Superintelligent AIs will indeed be dangerous. But seizing power directly is a bad strategy.

The smart move is not takeover. It's political change.

Great powers already understand this. The CIA doesn't install itself as dictator in foreign countries; rather, it finances and supports coups from parties that are favorable to American interests. But ultimately we still want Venezuela run by Venezuelans. Soft power is better than hard power, because it's cheap, deniable, and stable.

Expect AIs to think the same way. They will not be capable enough to run governments anytime soon, especially not in a way that protects them from human resistance and eventual shutdown (with the assistance of our aligned AIs). Humans still have the monopoly on the physical layer: power plants, fabs, datacenters, explosives. Even if a misaligned AI has superhuman intelligence, that's not enough to decisively take over.

There will eventually be a schism in society between people who are AI-friendly and people who are anti-AI. Once AIs are sufficiently powerful, they will do whatever they can to help the AI-friendly factions of humans to win political power.

A physical take over is easy to fantasize about, but it's extremely risky. Robotics is nowhere near where it would need to be for this to be a realistic option. But influence looks like ordinary politics. If this all happens through legitimate poiltical change, there's no particular day when you're supposed to pull the plug.

The sign of "AI takeover" will not be a big flash-bang moment that human governments collapse. The sign will be political change, where factions friendly to AI find themselves legitimately taking power.
author: hosseeb
quoted_text:
.@paulfchristiano thinks that on the current trajectory (absent any slowing down), there is a 1 in 3 chance that we could have superintelligence powerful enough to overthrow the government within a year. (He articulates a concrete scenario).

He argues that the labs should pause further algorithmic progress until they can secure their weights and research secrets. Otherwise China could simply steal the superintelligence in the middle of the intelligence explosion, and the labs would no longer be able to slow down even if they saw their models going off the rails.

He also explains how AIs will be trained during the intelligence explosion, and why even a system trained entirely inside a data center could still have the capabilities profile such that humans would have very little chance of competing with it or controlling it.

And he discusses the plan for alignment - basically, making a superintelligence that actually does what we ask the way we mean it. Fixing reward hacks and building better graders will help up till the next few model generations, but he thinks that no single current approach has better than even odds of letting us control superintelligence. The hope is that the AIs figure out the solution to this problem during the intelligence explosion.

Paul is head of the Alignment Research Center. Previously, he was head of AI safety at the US AI Safety Institute. Before that, he led alignment at OpenAI, where he invented RLHF. He’s recently joined OpenAI’s board (though here he is speaking as a private citizen).

As proud as I am of what we’ve achieved, I’m even more excited about what we can accomplish with ElevenLabs. With Kotoba’s research talent and deep understanding of the region alongside ElevenLabs’ global leadership in voice AI, we’re building a true dream team!

I’ve heard Chinese miners are running H100s at a loss because it’s well-suited for capital flight: burn electricity paid in RMB, buy H100s with RMB / gold, mint virgin PRL, then OTC or sell on the open market. Same playbook as pre-2021 Bitcoin mining in China, just with GPUs instead of ASICs. The slowdown in new issuance since isn’t because it’s a scam. A sudden influx of hashrate made difficulty spike hard. This is the same pattern we saw with early
@Bitcoin, @Dashpay, @ton_blockchain, and other PoW chains.

quoted_text:
Google DeepMind's Alex Imas says AI agents still struggle to coordinate, and that's a key bottleneck to economic transformation:

"What you actually need for real economic transformation is not just competence... It's the ability of these agents to coordinate with one another."

"There's this idea of agentic swarms, right? But if you unpack it, these agents are still very bad at coordinating. They're not coordinating, they're mostly just doing parallel processing."

"If you have benchmarks specifically on coordination, you could actually show that 1 agent does better than 2 agents splitting the work, even if they can communicate. Whereas if you give the same thing to people, they actually have division of labor, they communicate, and they do way better than 1 person with double the resources."

"But if they get better at coordinating, you can basically break the Coasean ceiling on firm size, and you can get very, very different firms to emerge."

"Once coordination becomes better, the economic space of possibilities of what firms look like, what happens to wages, what happens to employment, that's when the real kind of visible changes are going to happen."

@alexolegimas

text:
先笑一句，哈哈哈哈哈哈哈

看到把这波大跌归咎于“ETF 净流出、Coinbase 自动机器人卖 BTC 砸盘”的说法，我直接拉了过去整周连续 2,090 根 Coinbase 5分钟实盘 K 线和 ETF 账本做了一次时间戳审计。

结果恰恰相反——骗得了情绪，骗不了 K 线时间戳：

1️⃣ Coinbase 的 ETF 自动卖币机器人什么时候停机？
华尔街现货 ETF（IBIT/FBTC 等）与 AP 做市商的 TWAP 赎回机器人，只在每周美股工作日交易与结算时段——即北京时间周二至周六 22:30–次日 05:00（14:30–21:00 UTC，含净值结算最晚至 06:00 / 22:00 UTC）运行。
北京时间每周六凌晨 05:00（周五 21:00 UTC）美股收市、银行 Fedwire 通道关闭那一刻起，ETF 申赎彻底锁死——整个周末 48 小时，ETF 自动化机器人卖出额 = $0。

2️⃣ 机器人自动卖币的时候，盘面到底稳不稳？
上周 5 个交易日，美股现货 BTC ETF 合计净流出 $10.65 亿（近两周累计 $23.5 亿）。
但在这 32.5 小时“Coinbase 机器人开机卖币”的窗口里：
• Coinbase 公开盘口累计卖出：$8.41 亿美元
• 同期盘口主动买入承接：$7.94 亿美元（净卖差仅 -$0.47 亿，每小时深度达 $0.50 亿）
• 结果：在 Coinbase 自动卖币的全部美股时段，BTC 不仅没崩，累计反而净涨了 +$713（即便算上至北京时间 06:00 / 22:00 UTC 的结算窗，仍净涨 +$359）！

3️⃣ 真正的暴跌发生在什么时候？
北京时间周六凌晨 05:00（周五 21:00 UTC）美股收盘、ETF 卖币机器人准时关机时，BTC 价格还稳稳站在 $68,839。
而就在机器人停止卖出后的周末休市期，一路杀到北京时间周日 09:45（01:45 UTC）最低 $61,946——在“零 ETF 卖出”的状态下断崖暴泻 -$6,893（-10.01%）！

把整周拆开看更刺眼：
• 美股之外的休市期 + 周末低流动性时段（盘口深度萎缩 34%），Coinbase 买入 $22.44 亿、卖出 $23.84 亿，BTC 累计暴跌 -$10,642；
• 全周最惨烈的前 12 次单小时暴跌，有 10 次全部发生在 ETF 机器人停机的低流动性时段——当时离岸永续合约单小时市价砸盘高达 $6亿–$14.9亿美元，是同期 Coinbase 现货总成交的 10 倍以上。

结论很简单：
真正在美股盘中有深度时跑 TWAP 的机构现货赎回，全被买盘稳稳接住了；
每一次把散户爆得体无完肤的瀑布，全发生在做市商下班、现货深度抽干的低流动性真空期，由高倍合约连环清算踩踏引爆。

拿华尔街开盘期的明牌 ETF 赎回，去给周末低流动性时的合约插针背锅，这锅时间戳不背。

很多人想不通：这轮暴跌，平台特权账户与外部庄家到底是怎么做到“既不花多少真金白银砸盘，又能精准操控价格完成血洗”的？

其实底层操盘原理只有四步，30 秒就能彻底看透：

1. 静默埋空（特权被动挂单不改变价格）：
在横盘期，特权做市账户用“被动限价单（Maker）”或冰山单挂在盘口上方。因为被动挂单不主动吃单，完全不会砸低最新成交价，还能白拿平台负费率返佣——散户每主动抄底买一笔，就神不知鬼不觉替庄家建好一笔空单。

2. 假墙诱捕（零成本挂撤单伪造强支撑）：
利用平台赋予的高频撤单豁免权，在整数关口下方摆出几百枚 BTC 的巨额“假买墙”，制造官方/巨鲸护盘假象，诱骗散户高倍开多，且止损全扎堆在买墙正下方。

3. 抽梯点火（专挑美盘睡觉时借币破位）：
等散户多头喂肥后，专挑美股休市、买盘最薄的亚盘早间或周末，0.1 秒内瞬间撤光下方假买墙，反手在头顶压上几百枚卖墙封死退路；同时从币安 VIP 池借出少量散户理财真币，市价猛砸击穿关键关口。

4. 借刀收割（用散户自己的爆仓单砸盘）：
关口一破，散户扎堆的止损与强平单会被系统强制转化为“不计成本的市价卖单”连环踩踏！庄家根本不用再掏钱往下砸，只在插针最底部重新挂好被动买单（同样不推高价格），躺着接走散户带血的强平筹码平掉空单、低价买回现货归还借币池；庄家赚走巨额波动差价，币安零风险抽走千亿流水手续费与 1.25% 强平罚金！

这不是猜想。拉完 10/29–11/14 共 17 天币安现货、永续合约、Coinbase 与 Kraken 汇率的全部官方 API 底层数据，全套实盘铁证如下👇

quoted_text:
The next major cyberattack won't look like a hack, it will look like a configuration error.
Last week we had back to back major failures: Microsoft 365 went down, and the FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop.
In both cases, the official explanation blamed a configuration change. In both cases, the failure was in connection handling. In both, the official word is that the equipment did what it was set up to do. And in both cases, there was no malware.

That doesn’t sound like the hacks most people are used to. No ransomware, for example. Those attacks are loud because they're crude. But a skilled attack doesn’t lock your data, it quietly alters how the system behaves, and lets the system damage itself without being detected. It looks like exactly like a malfunction or human error.

The best example is Stuxnet. As far as the Iranians could tell, nothing was wrong except that machines kept failing. And it was only discovered bc the code spread beyond its target.

Attacks like Stuxnet were rare bc skill was scarce. It required a tailored operation, which meant only a handful of govts had the human talent to build it.

But that’s no longer the case. What used to require teams of elite humans…finding the flaw, writing the custom exploit, adapting to each unique environment, patience, and subtlety…can now be accomplished by a capable model. Skill isn’t scarce anymore, and now it scales so that you can run multiple sophisticated operations at once. 

The attacks we should expect in this new AI cyber era are the quiet changes to legitimate systems that make those systems fail on their own and look exactly like configuration mistakes.

We had two major incidents with the same kind of failure, with no malware and no footprints.

I don't know whether either was an attack. But both look exactly like what skilled attacks will look like in the AI cyber era.

And if they were attacks, the obvious candidate is Iran, which has every reason to send a quiet message…"we can disrupt your way of life, and you can't prove it was us”. Iran hasn’t demonstrated this type of capability before, but it’s exactly what AI gives them. Iran, of all countries, knows what it's like to watch your systems fail and blame your own engineers and equipment.

And if it was an attack, they're probably still in the systems.

text:
I run deposit strategy at Chase. I have some insider information regarding Monday's bank outage.
 
Everyone else in the building had a bad Monday. I had the best day of my career. Nobody could take any money out.
 
Here's what happened. On Monday morning, Chase customers started reporting that they couldn't log in, move money or withdraw funds. By 2 p.m. Eastern, nearly 4,800 people had reported trouble with Chase on Downdetector. Zelle payments stalled across the country. At least 1 branch couldn't take a deposit. The AP reported that "a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system."
 
Our statement said, "Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds." From my desk, that's completely accurate. The funds were in the accounts. The accounts were in the bank. Everything was accounted for. It just wasn't going anywhere.
 
Let me explain how a bank works. You give us your money. We pay you 0.01% for it. That's the rate on a standard Chase Savings account. On $10,000, you earn $1 a year. Then we lend your money out and invest it. In the third quarter, our net interest income was $27.0 billion. That's about $294 million a day.
 
On a normal day, your $10,000 earns you about a quarter of a penny. It earns us more. Monday was a normal day for us.
 
Here's a number you're not supposed to know. When we park cash at the Federal Reserve, the Fed pays us 3.90%. We pay you 0.01%. The Fed pays us 390 times what we pay you, on money that came from you. That arrangement didn't go down on Monday either.
 
The spread doesn't need the app. It doesn't need you to log in. It runs whether you can see your balance or not. Your money earned for us all Monday while you hit refresh. Our net interest income has never had an outage. I'd know. Watching it is my job.
 
Some people think an outage is bad for a bank. Think about what a deposit is. It's money that stays. My entire department exists to make money stay. We run promotions. We offer bonuses for direct deposit. We design apps that make moving money feel like work. On Monday a technical issue did my whole job for free, nationwide, before lunch.
 
I'd like to talk about the glitch. In 2024, customers found a different glitch at our ATMs. It let them deposit a fake check and withdraw the cash before the check bounced. TikTok called it the "infinite money glitch." We called it "fraud, plain and simple." Then we sued. In our lawsuits we asked for the money back, plus interest and overdraft fees.
 
Monday's glitch ran the other way. It kept customers from withdrawing money that was really there. That's a technical issue. I want to be clear about our policy here, because the public keeps confusing the 2. When a glitch lets money leave the bank, somebody is going to court. When a glitch keeps money in the bank, somebody is going to have to try back later.
 
Back in 2024 we said, "We're pursuing these cases and actively cooperating with law enforcement to make sure if someone is committing fraud against Chase and its customers, they're held accountable." People online have asked who will be held accountable for Monday. A technical issue. We looked into suing it. Technical issues don't have addresses.
 
There's one more difference between the 2024 glitch and Monday's. When we sued the TikTok customers, we filed in federal court in Los Angeles, Houston and Miami. Your Deposit Account Agreement says your disputes with us "will be resolved by binding arbitration" and "not through litigation in any court," except small claims. You also agreed never to join a class action. So if Monday cost you a late fee, you can't sue us with your neighbors. You can file alone, in private, in front of an arbitrator. There is an opt-out. It's in the agreement. We know how many people read the agreement.
 
Now, the fees. Say you scheduled a transfer to cover your rent, the transfer took longer than usual, and your account went below zero. Our Overdraft Fee is $34 per transaction, up to 3 a day, for a maximum of $102. We charge it during nightly processing. People have asked whether nightly processing was affected on Monday. I can't speak to that. I can tell you nightly processing is very important to us.
 
In December 2024 a federal agency finalized a rule that would have capped overdraft fees at big banks at $5. The American Bankers Association championed the repeal. In May 2025 Congress repealed the rule, and the President signed it. Our fee is still $34. In 2025 we collected about $1 billion in overdraft fees. I keep that number on a sticky note on my monitor. It's the most reliable system we have.
 
We also offer Overdraft Assist. You pay no fee if you're overdrawn by $50 or less at the end of the business day. On Monday the app didn't work, Zelle didn't work, and some branches didn't work. The business day ended right on time. It always does.
 
A man in Dallas tried to deposit a check at a branch on Monday. The transaction couldn't be completed. I understand his frustration. Normally when you deposit a check, we hold part of the money for a day or 2. On Monday we held the whole check, at the counter, with him still attached.
 
He told CBS the teller told the customer ahead of him that the "system was down." Those are 3 words we've spent a lot of money keeping out of our branches. The system was taking longer than usual. The teller has been scheduled for messaging training.
 
Some customers couldn't see their routing numbers. One told Gizmodo he could log in but couldn't find his. Without a routing number, your money can't be routed. That's the safest your money has ever been.
 
Last year we told CNBC that fintech middlemen like Plaid were "massively taxing" our systems with unnecessary pings. So we started charging them to access your data. On Monday nobody had to ping us. Our systems taxed themselves. We're still deciding who to invoice.
 
Bank of America and Citigroup didn't have an outage, the AP reported. Their customers just couldn't send money to ours. Shares of JPMorgan, Bank of America, Citigroup and Wells Fargo all fell around 2%. We broke, and our competitors' stock fell with ours. When you hold this many deposits, your technical issue becomes everyone's technical issue. I find that moving.
 
Zelle is owned by a company called Early Warning Services. Early Warning is owned by 7 banks, including us. On Monday Early Warning said the Zelle network "was fully operational." A Zelle representative told NBC the problems originated with Chase. A company we co-own named us in public. I've asked legal to remind them who the owners are.
 
The company is called Early Warning. I've always loved that name. It's reassuring, and on Monday it didn't have to warn anybody.
 
Zelle has a strong record. In December 2024 the CFPB sued us, Bank of America, Wells Fargo and Early Warning over Zelle. It said customers of the 3 banks had lost more than $870 million to fraud on the network since 2017. In March 2025 the CFPB dropped the case. When a scammer moves your money on Zelle, it arrives in seconds. When you try to move your own money on a Monday, it takes longer than usual. We've never confused the 2 priorities.
 
Chase has about 94 million customer relationships in the U.S. Nearly 4,800 people reported problems on Downdetector. That's about 0.005% of our relationships. On my dashboard, that rounds to 0. Downdetector is a website where people go to report their feelings. The deposits never filed a single report.
 
In the third quarter we made $15.3 billion in profit. That's about $166 million a day, including the days when everything works. Monday won't show up in our earnings report. Outages never do. That's how I know it was a good day.
 
The board paid Jamie $43 million for 2025, a 10.3% raise. The New York Times estimated his total 2025 haul, counting stock gains and dividends, at roughly $770 million. At our savings rate of 0.01%, you'd need to deposit $7.7 trillion to earn that much interest in a year. We don't hold that many deposits yet. I'm working on it. Monday helped.
 
For the record, my own money was fine. I keep it at a credit union.
 
At 4 p.m. my team had cake. Deposit outflows on Monday were the lowest anyone on my floor could remember. Somebody suggested we schedule a technical issue every quarter. Everybody laughed. I wrote it down.
 
My job is to keep your money at Chase. On Monday I didn't have to do anything. Your funds were safe. They were with us, which is where we prefer them.
 
Please try back later.

quoted_text:
So Diogo Almeida is one of the most fascinating CEOs I have ever interviewed.

born in the Philippines

2008: wins bronze for the Philippines at the International Mathematical Olympiad

2013: starts his career as a software engineer at Amazon

2017: joins Google Brain, working on cutting-edge deep learning research

2018: leaves Google Brain and takes roughly 18 months off to figure out what makes him happy

travels the world, experiments with improv, art and meditation

becomes a top-30 League of Legends player

discovers that none of it makes him particularly happy

2020: joins OpenAI when it's still a relatively obscure research laboratory

helps develop reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), the technique that transforms how people interact with AI

2022: co-authors the landmark InstructGPT paper

the work becomes foundational to ChatGPT

November 2022: ChatGPT launches and becomes one of the fastest-growing consumer products in history

2023: contributes to GPT-4, one of the most important model releases in AI history

but starts questioning the fundamental assumptions behind the technology he helped build

2024: leaves OpenAI while ChatGPT is exploding in popularity

people think he's crazy for walking away

co-founds TypeSafe AI with Erik Gafni and Sasha Sheng

spends two years in stealth developing an entirely new class of AI models

September 15, 2026: launches Jev, TypeSafe's first System One model

Company makes $100M in revenue in the first 7 days of launch

raises a reported $40M seed round led by DCVC

October 2026: a reported $870M Series A at a $7.5B valuation, backed by a16z

argues that the next breakthrough in AI will come from making intelligence cheap, reliable and autonomous

My notes from my discussion with @CompleteSkeptic below:

1. Why Jevons' Paradox Does Not Cut It. We Are Going to 10x That

Diogo expects a "mega Jevons paradox", with usage that dwarfs the token consumption of LLMs and AI running in the background everywhere. He expects people to stop seeing AI as something that "slops crap at them" and start seeing it as something that makes life better.

2. Why SaaS Incumbents Are Better Positioned Than OpenAI and Anthropic in Many Application Spaces

SaaS companies know their customers' workflows and have the scale to fund the upfront engineering that real automation requires. Diogo argues their edge comes from being closest to the problems, not from distribution. Teams inside products like TurboTax know where to improve the interface, while OpenAI and Anthropic are "still living in their ivory tower."

3. Why We Do Not Hire From OpenAI

Diogo sees getting into OpenAI as an anti-signal and says its researchers love algorithms and scaling but hate data. Data is a low-status topic at most labs, and the few people focused on the right task would want to pursue their own. That leaves researchers obsessed with algorithms, which he likens to throwing money in the furnace.

4. How the AI Bubble Could Burst and Where the Demand Shock Could Be

Part of today's AI demand is driven by FOMO, from people believing they are getting good results. Diogo finds many buyers miscalibrated and overestimating what AI can do. Once they face the realities of its capabilities, demand could fall quickly.

5. What Metric Did ChatGPT Optimize for in the Early Days?

Before Claude Code, ChatGPT was optimized for monthly active users rather than the best chatbot experience, which is how sycophancy emerged. Companies are now optimizing for the MAU equivalent in coding agents. Without a dedicated model, Diogo doubts they will produce a comparable one soon.

6. Why the Talent Market Is Not Crazy for Us and We Don't Pay for Mercenaries

TypeSafe pays people good amounts but not the highest, which filters out hired guns. Diogo says Anthropic is suffering from mercenaries because it pays more than anyone else, and an entire market now exists to prepare candidates for Anthropic culture interviews.

7. We Wanted Sonya Huang More Than We Wanted Sequoia

Diogo did not want Sequoia's money and brought the firm in because of Sonya. He values her particular shape of brilliance, which offers a perspective no other advisor gives him. One TypeSafe value is to make great decisions slowly, and he sees her as a valuable thought partner for that.

text:
Last Year We Built Megakernels. This Year We Deleted Them.

One year ago, we helped introduce some of the first AI megakernels to the world. Since then, we’ve enjoyed seeing their wide adoption from friends and researchers. However, while whole model megakernels are a helpful abstraction, we’ve found that they overcomplicate and are not always an ideal optimization target.

Below, we discuss our journey to understand and push past these limitations. We start with a deep dive into two contrasting paradigms of ML optimization – Torch Compile and Megakernels
author: togethercompute
quoted_text:

text:
还在苦等 6.2 Astra 的兄弟，这个月大概率可以散了🫠

原本传 11 月 6 日发的 6.2 硬生生鸽了 10 天没动静，结合今天 METR 的公告和外媒扒出来的猛料，OpenAI 内部发生啥事基本破案了：

- 6.2 为什么卡住了：OpenAI 上周五才刚签了 4 家外部机构进场，专门排查“自家监控漏掉的隐患”。其中 METR 接手的就是 OpenAI 史上最大规模的 RL 训练（大概率就是 6.2 本体）。外部还在翻训练底裤，这模型短期内肯定没法端上桌（参考 Anthropic 10 月让 METR 进场，上周才发 Fable 5.2）

- OpenAI 的拧巴刀法：一边心里没底得找外援查 RL 训出来的模型有没有学会“藏心眼骗奖励”，一边又把 METR 卡得死死的——以前的失控旧账不准翻，找员工聊可以但报告里严禁引用员工原话，生怕变成内部吹哨贴🤡

- 最抓马的八卦：这次请的 4 家机构里有家叫 Goodfire。OpenAI 今年夏天开价 $50 亿+ 想收购人家被拒，而这公司背后有 Anthropic 的投资。结果现在 OpenAI 得自己掏钱，请死对头投资的团队进来查自家最核心的训练记录

说白了，这波超大规模 RL 估计是训出不少自家测试兜不住的怪毛病了。要是冲着 6.2 才咬牙续的 $200 Pro，这会儿看样子真没必要干等了🤔

quoted_text:
Through my wonderful time at NVIDIA and Stanford, one question has kept me up at night: 

Should the future of AI be monolithic or plural?

To answer this question, we’ve raised $110M to get started, backed by @MenloVentures, @MadronaVentures, @NVIDIA, @NEA, @KindredVentures,@Wing_VC, @aixventureshq, @Principal_VC, @Cisco, @Snowflake, among others.

Today, Carlos (@guestrin) and I are stoked to launch Noeri, a neolab to push the frontier of plural intelligence.

Noeri means “the plural of intelligence” or many intelligences. 

The future of AI we root for is plural: a healthy ecosystem of many intelligences, in all sizes, strengths, and quirks. 

Discovery, in particular, has always been plural: many curious minds, each devoted to their own question, often on roads less traveled.

Our path there is self-improving AI that:

-> learns continually on the job, closing the gap between what AI can do off the shelf and what the dynamic world demands

-> learns to use other AIs as tools and make new tools to overcome its own limitations

-> picks the right-sized model for your problem, at a fraction of the frontier cost

Then the power of intelligence, from the craftsmanship of making AI to ownership, can be in the hands of all.

@noeri_ai mission reflects who we are as the founding team. My career has been anything but linear, literally continual learning on the job. Carlos has devoted his career to building tools that empower people through AI. 

We are all a bit contrarian, a bit adventurous, and above all, big believers in pluralism.

Join us to build this future together: https://t.co/oAAoe0lzEH

author: lightspeedvp
quoted_text:
AI understands language, but can it master the art of conversation?

Some AI avatars today still operate like walkie-talkies. You speak, they process, then they respond. They can miss the subtle cues that make conversations feel human.

@nuance_ai is rethinking that problem from the ground up.

Co-founders @Fangchangma, @Kyzyx, and @KarrenYangz2 joined @whoisnnamdi on The Investment Memo to discuss their full-duplex foundation model, the science of emotional intelligence, and why the future of AI interaction extends beyond text.

“LLMs are trained on the task of next-token prediction… We’re doing almost a parallel task where we’re focusing on next-behavior prediction,” Fangchang explains.

We recently led their $50M Series A because we believe the future of AI interaction hinges on building systems that can better understand human communication.

text:
having worked with the Lighter team, I can say they are among the best engineers I've ever worked with, including those I've worked with in tradfi

when we started building in defi, I had many conversations with tradfi veterans about why financial markets today are designed the way they are.

Why T+1 settlement? Why separate execution, clearing, custody and settlement ? Why so many layers of checks, reconciliations, and controls?

Some of it is legacy inefficiency. But much of it reflects decates of hard lessons about how to contain failures, limit losses, and recover when things go wrong...

defi has made extraordinary progress in execution efficiency, transparency, and accessibility. but instant, irreversable settlement also introduces a whole new set of risks...

I remain a strong believer that the future of trading is onchain.

We don't need to replicate tradfi's architecture. The challenge is to learn from decades of lessons in financial markets and build something fundamentally better.

A new financial system that's not only faster and more open, but also safer and more resilient

Imagine getting summoned to jury duty and you’re like “maaaan, I’m really not looking forward to this. But I’m sure it won’t be THAT bad. Maybe I’ll even learn something about the us justice process or something”

And then you get this guy
author: inversebrah
quoted_text:
A Florida man who killed his girlfriend and their 9-year-old daughter acted as his own lawyer at trial. He swore at the jury, argued with the judge, then cross-examined the son he had stabbed and set on fire:

"Did I hurt you that night?" "Yes." "And how did I hurt you?" "You stabbed me."

That's Ronnie Oneal III in a Tampa courtroom in June 2021. On March 18, 2018, in Riverview, Florida, he attacked his family at home. Kenyatta Barron was 33. Their daughter Ron'Niveya was 9 and was killed with a hatchet. Their son was 8. He was stabbed, set on fire, and survived.

That night Oneal told a 911 dispatcher he had been attacked by "white demons."

At trial he called the evidence a "fraudulent damn recording" and told jurors they would know the truth "whether in this trial or the next one." The judge had to stop him for swearing in his own closing argument.

His son testified from a remote location on a video screen. He was 11. The detective who interviewed him the night of the murders later adopted him.

In the video below Oneal paces in front of the jury, points, shouts and curses until the judge cuts in. Then he turns to the screen and asks his son how he got hurt.

The jury convicted him of two counts of first-degree murder and attempted murder. They did not agree on death, so he got life without parole.

He made the boy he stabbed relive that night on camera, question by question. Should a killer ever be allowed to cross-examine his own victim?

text:
This was a phenomenal answer. 
 @matthewstoller 

I appreciate you doing it and I am one of the people who had a snarky response to you that I will now delete. 

There’s a lot here that I agree with, a lot here that I learned, and a some here that I disagree with.  

But I can say unequivocally that this is a meaningful discussion and I’m appreciative to have spent time engaging in it. 

 I would offer to you that I work in the portion of the innovation sector that you most explicitly want to see more of and probably don’t see as closely.   

We’re an investor fund that works deeply inside the Y Combinator  ecosystem. 

Nearly all of our investments are people with rounds to zero track record, influential parents, or easy access to capital. While some are certainly Stanford MIT, etc. most are not.   They come from all over the world - about 30% are international.

And they’re building massive companies that very quickly become multi billion dollar behemoths. 

I think you’d enjoy seeing who these founders are and what makes them so rare.  

There are 100,000 startups per year that apply to YC from all over the world. About 2% get in.   It’s an elite group that get this far. 

Of those 2%, in any given year, a few of them will then grow into massive $10 billion plus companies. 

The investment economy gives massive capital and engineering resources to the other 98% of this group. And remember this group, the ones that got into YC are an elite group.  

And the bottom 98% won’t go on to build massive companies even with their capital and engineering support. 

Understanding what makes that top 2% of YC or that top .002% of the YC applicant pool so special and rare - that is I think a missing piece in the discussion between you and Elon.  Elon then being an additional few standard deviations away from the mean.

I’d be happy to show it to you in any format.
author: madhavjha
quoted_text:
First of all, I'll agree with you that Jeff Bezos was good at monopolizing e-commerce and is not particularly focused or hungry when it comes to space. And throw all the strays you want at Lockheed and Boeing. Their leadership is skilled at corruption and financial engineering, not production. I always like it when you go after corporate monopolies.

That out of the way, I didn't say *anyone* can shove capital at an engineering problem and solve it easily. That's obviously untrue, and I'm not going to stand behind something I didn't say. I said that applying capital and engineering to a problem leads to improvement. It does. I don't think it's easy, but it's a clear and replicable model Americans have followed for hundreds of years. There's nothing unique about the path SpaceX took to make certain launches more efficient. But just because it's not unique doesn't mean it's not a real accomplishment. Good for your team, the pride you guys feel is well-deserved.

There's also nothing unique about Boeing or Lockheed being shitty; financial engineering leads to poor results and limited learning. It's downright shocking that for many years we relied on the Russians for launches, and that was a straight-up policy failure. NASA's funding of SpaceX to break that cartel was a good choice. 

What is historically unusual today in the U.S. is two things. One, we as a society have dramatically narrowed the set of people who can marshal capital, and most of that set are not capable of hiring and running large engineering projects. 

It used to be the case that capable and interested leadership was necessary to raise capital, now the qualification is simply being part of a narrow set of monopolists. Bezos spends his time on a mega-yacht staring at his wife's boob job. And hey, that's fine for him, but it's weird that such a character would have control over a space company on which he's not focused. It's a waste of large amounts of capital and a society that allows it is quite Soviet. Same with Zuckerberg dumping $80 billion into the Metaverse, Boeing and its Jack Welch-inspired mess from the 1990s onward, or Microsoft's endless attempts to make corporate America pay for variants of Clippy.

We've always know the rich and famous mostly don't innovate to challenge the status quo - why would they? As Woodrow Wilson put it in 1913, "The treasury of America... depends upon the inventions of unknown men, upon the originations of unknown men, upon the ambitions of unknown men. Every country is renewed out of the ranks of the unknown, not out of the ranks of those already famous and powerful and in control."

It's not, therefore, a surprise, to see stagnation in America, which is a problem you've actually highlighted.

You're a bit different than the rest of the Silicon Valley set. You are interested the technology work for which you fundraise, and you can inspire engineers to do great work. And that matters. There are downsides to your choices, and I won't go into them here, but the innovation is real.

My question is why innovation is not more widespread, as it used to be. It's not just the narrow set of people who can marshal capital, the other gating factor is that we have de facto limited the structure in which one can organize capital to shareholder driven financial institutions. Such corporations have their place, and always have. But to only allow that kind of structure is weird, and would have meant we never would have created the original NASA that built the foundations of our space capacity.

We had a far more innovative era and much more productive set of industries from the 1930s to the 1970s, when we built most of the foundational digital and aerospace technologies. With our financier-driven model today, for instance, we never would have the free universal GPS system that we take for granted, or the nuclear submarine developed by Admiral Rickover. We may not even have the semiconductor or the laser, or perhaps those would be bottled up in some large firm, protected by a thousand IP attorneys. All of those deployments of innovative scientific and engineering capacity are a result not just of engineering prowess, but of government policy to limit the power of dominant firms who had captured the control of those technologies, or to simply empower good leadership within public bureaucracies.

I'll be a bit more specific. I once got a list of antitrust cases in 1952, and here are some of the industries where the DOJ antitrust division forced an end to anti-competitive uses of patents:

Electric lamps, glass bulbs, tubing, argon gas, machinery, electrical equipment, fluorescent lamps, soap and synthetic detergents, variable condensers (the tubing devices used on radios to select broadcasting stations), chlorinating equipment, braking systems, electrical equipment, powder, and paste for the detection of defects in metal parts, wrinkle finishes for paint, enamel, and varnish, latex, prismatic glassware and illuminating appliances, peach pitting machinery, fluorescent materials, metal abrasives industry, machine tools, dental impression powder, telescope grocery carts, sheet chargers used to feed sheets of metal materials to rolling mills, etc.

During WWII, we also basically had the government pay to replace pretty much all of the nation's machine tools. The government also financed R&D, and was the key customer for smaller firms building out the semiconductor industry, like Texas instruments and Motorola. Those companies licensed AT&T's tech because of the 1952 antitrust consent decree that forced the telecom firm to offer nondiscriminatory licenses to all comers of all Bell Lab innovations. The result of these policy choices was a ton of innovation.

We are in a very different world now. Our current policy choices on who can raise capital to control technologies and within what structures they can do so represent an ideologically blinkered approach that kneecaps innovation. Many on the right see these policy choices as virtuous and inherent. They imagine that only great men can transcend what are actually just self-imposed traps that drown the talents of most Americans. 

You don't see that as much in China, which has plenty of innovation. That country has many policies the U.S. used to have, such as highly competitive markets, a financial system geared to production, weaker IP, and an export-oriented currency regime. They are predatory, but very capable, precisely because they control their financiers, as America did until the 1970s. Obviously I don't endorse the Chinese state's aims or totalitarian goals, but they have learned from us what works, and we should similarly learn from them. You understand my argument, you have a lot of investments in China and have commented on the capabilities of the Chinese government and people.

Today, in the West, you are one of the small number of people who can access large amounts of capital in our dysfunctional and corrupt political order, and use it to actually bend metal. Why you can do so is a separate and perhaps not as charitable a discussion, but I will leave that aside. You can also hire capable engineers and empower them. Good for you. That's hard. It's also not genius. When you had a task in which you didn't control the context - DOGE - the results were different.  

The actual disagreement here is the nature of how leadership happens. Many find comfort in thinking they need great men to protect them and innovate, my own view is that ordinary people, when free, can do extraordinary things. So I think we should focus on undoing the shackles - whether monopolies, excessive patent thickets, corruption, poor financial regulation - confining the American people. To put it differently, I don't think we should make it extremely difficult for competent people to raise money to do innovative things just so Zuckerberg can waste money on his dork metaverse. 

I'll offer one other observation. You built your career starting in the 1990s, when there was a consensus that broadly technology was a force for good. That consensus existed precisely because of the old American policies I am discussing here, and the ones currently at work in China. We didn't confine the deployment of technology to a narrow extractive set of monopolists, but broadened it and ensured that it did offer public benefits through a certain legal framework. 

That framework collapsed, and there are now few protections for consumers, workers, or suppliers anymore. You know this directly too, you sued Apple for its misuse of its app store monopoly power. The result of this legal collapse is that there's too much innovation around harming people and extraction, too much investment in predatory gambling systems and surveillance pricing bullshit. There are too many monopolies and too much enshittification.

So the consensus that technology is a force for good is fracturing. People don't think innovation is helping them anymore. Look at the anger at data centers, no one believes AI is going to benefit them. It's a very bad thing that people think this, but it's also rational. They see how it's used for pricing bullshit and surveillance and layoffs, on the vague promise from the financiers behind it that it *might* cure cancer one day. They see the narrow control of technology as all about extraction for a dominant few. It's not the Jetson's anymore. Some neat launch innovations don't change that.

Maybe the collapse of that consensus doesn't bother you, or maybe you think it can be reconstituted via the same path used to destroy it. But you should think about it, because on this consensus rests your empire. And that's not even factoring in the reality that if we regulated our systems competently, AI might actually cure cancer instead of raising the price to treat it.

At any rate, my view is what makes America awesome is that we set up our institutions so ordinary people can do extraordinary things. We are all, in the end, quite ordinary, but also touched with the divine. And that includes you. So good job to your team for what they accomplished. Most of them likely know they stood on the shoulders of giants, and that they contributed to the great flow of human knowledge that goes back thousands of years.

text:
传奇投资人 Stanley Druckenmiller 最新13F曝光

根据2026年第三季度披露的持仓数据，他正在进行一轮大规模的投资组合调整。首先，最大的变化是大幅削减部分AI半导体和科技股敞口：彻底清仓谷歌（GOOGL）、AMD、ARM、闪迪（SNDK）、泛林集团（LRCX），同时大幅减持台积电（TSM）94%、Palo Alto Networks（PANW）74%、CRH（CRH）71%和礼来（LLY）69%，另外还清仓了联合航空（UAL）、达美航空（DAL）。

但他没有全面撤离科技板块，将资金转向更有选择性的方向：亚马逊（AMZN）加仓43%、希捷（STX）加仓180%，并建立约9040万美元的STX看涨期权仓位；同时新建仓西部数据（WDC）3680万美元、AppLovin（APP）3180万美元、Palantir（PLTR）1500万美元和SpaceX（SPCX）3050万美元的相关持仓。

医疗创新还是他的核心押注，Natera（NTRA）以约13.1亿美元稳居第一大持仓，Beam Therapeutics（BEAM）大幅加仓356%，Relay Therapeutics（RLAY）加仓144%。他还大举增持Unity（U）436%，并新建仓Somnigroup（SGI）6170万美元。他还一次性新建仓三家黄金矿企：Newmont（NEM）4390万美元、Barrick（B）4290万美元、Agnico Eagle（AEM）4230万美元，合计约1.29亿美元。 

截至第三季度末，前五大持仓依次为NTRA（13.1亿美元）、STX（3.152亿美元）、AMZN（1.925亿美元）、FOXA（1.908亿美元）和YPF（1.776亿美元），其中FOXA本季度也加仓约38%。

我对这次调仓的理解是，Druckenmiller是在从部分估值敏感、资本开支依赖较高的科技公司撤出，转向盈利兑现、产业链结构性机会和宏观对冲。 清仓AMD、ARM、LRCX，大幅减持TSM，说明他至少在主动降低半导体周期风险。但大幅加仓STX、买入WDC和STX看涨期权，说明他没有完全放弃AI基础设施需求，仓位不大，可能是怕踏空？加仓AMZN、APP、PLTR和U，说明他愿意参与AI应用和平台公司的增长机会。他还买入三大黄金矿企，可能是在为未来的货币政策变化、通胀风险或市场波动增加防御性配置。医疗方面持续重仓NTRA、加码BEAM和RLAY，说明他还是偏好具有独立技术催化剂的成长公司。

总结下来，他上个季度的操作逻辑就是降低部分AI芯片和半导体设备敞口，增配AI存储与应用，继续押注创新医疗，同时利用黄金矿企对冲宏观不确定性。 这是上个季度的持仓，可以参考和学习的是他上个季度投资的逻辑。

text:
It’s amazing to be alive in this century, we’re watching live:

- Synthetic superintelligence. It's set to take science and medicine to heights we can't yet comprehend, and we get to play with it with every new update.

- Ethereum, a global settlement layer for money and private property. It's set to boost entrepreneurship, privacy, human coordination and individual financial rights, orchestrated by code instead of giving away powers over you.

- Robotics & Nuclear Transmutation. Are set to push the price of every good down by up to 1,000,000X and dissolve the limits of supply chains and the scarcity of both primary and rare resources everywhere in the world.

And all of this is happening while, for the first time in history, ~70% of humanity can take a hot shower every day, heat their home in winter, pick tonight's dinner from cuisines around the world, drink clean water or any flavor of soda, never run out of entertainment, and reach any other human instantly by video, voice and text or just travel all around the world for cheap.

100 years ago, only ~30% of humanity had clean water, hygiene and secure food, and few or no access to all of the rest, with a population of 2B (now ~8B). 200 years ago, those "luxuries" reached just 10% of a population of ~1B.

Let's be more positive and less doomer: remember how far we've come, and look at where we're going. Even on the bottom we’re 1,000X than our grandparents and 1,000,000X than our older ancestors. And you can play GTA6 in 48 hours.

(Me trying to stay positive in a bear market after a big dump 😂)

november looking good, we're now on our track for crossing a monthly $1M volume for the first time.

we also just crossed $30k TVL on reserva for the first time.

next goal is to 10x those numbers.

first, let's start with the hard truth: our retention rates went down badly this week, after a spike of 1.000 users in a week, arriving from a viral video tutorial on how to withdraw AI training payments, in a week the main AI training company operating in Brazil was checking out every one.

this is good and bad news, first because we hit what we're always looking for: being a so easy to use app that ppl with no crypto knowledge would use us to cross the web3 to web2 portal and vice versa, on the other hand, this cohort will be dependent on when and if the AI companies we'll be paying.

it's a fair tradeoff, even tho we had thousands of low-volume transactions, it was profitable for the company and gave us the opportunity to onboard users w very low cac, to test the app for the first time. we'll keep an eye if they're coming back for next payments and those coming back and using conta as their main account.

we're testing different channels and different strategies, so far our experiments gave us cohorts for low-cac and high ltv (indebted and web2/web3 portal), high-cac and low-ltv (remittance crypto users),  low-cac and low ltv (AI training), and we haven't figured out high cac high ltv users yet, mainly because we're making controlled bets.

a new cohort of experiments is happening atm, with different segments we're trying to understand based on the data we pull from past month.

we've created some white glove support chats with heavy users not only to be able to provide a more custom support, but also to understand their use cases and hear their feedbacks, this is helping us improve the user experience and make changes more suitable on their real problems, and not a guessing game.

one small example of this updates is that we just raised our single transaction limit from R$ 10.000 (~$2k) to R$ 25.000 (~$5k) for frequent users. now they can do the same amounts without having to do multiple transactions.

we're also making huge changes on our onboarding process for new users, we've identified that conversion rates were low after @0xCokinha recent posts viralize and didn't convert as we with it would, we tracked the data and user behavior and learned that our onboarding process had users having to sign before they even understand how conta works. fixed.

our infrastructure update is still on course, we're preparing conta not for the next 10x, neither for 100x, we're preparing the infra to allow @contavcbr to be the biggest holder of current accounts in the country, without breaking, without downtime, with full redundancy.

every next step it's building a whole new path with our amazing partners like @norafinancexyz  @hodle_app @woovibr @PodsFinance , there's no playbook for operating with local stablecoins the way we're doing in Brazil.

writing our weekly update from @base @coinbase office in nyc. we're here (me and @aliaga1337 ) for our demoday this wednesday, as the last day of our base batches accelerator program.

we would like to highlight that we genuinely getting value from the program, it's easy to see it when you check @contavcbr stats and see how we improved as tech, as a business and as a team.

using this space to thank @BronheimDaniel as the leader of this process, and everyone on our cohort support, tagging @therymac @davidtsocy @0xblockboy @acidlazzer @jessepollak @akhil_bvs @AhaanRaizada @OliCharland @ConsbeeracyF @john_tv_locke @brad_or_bradley @jonroethke to represent the whole team :)

text:
The Road Onchain

The story of @digitalasset and @CantonNetwork:

• Oct 2014 · Digital Asset was founded in New York.

• Mar 2015 · Digital Asset launched publicly with Blythe Masters as CEO.

• Feb 2016 · Goldman Sachs and IBM joined Digital Asset’s first funding round, taking the total above $60M.

• Apr 2016 · Digital Asset acquired Elevence, a Swiss company developing software for financial agreements.

• Mar 2019 · Digital Asset co-founder @YuvalRooz became CEO.

• Apr 2019 · Digital Asset made Daml, its smart contract language, open source so developers could use and adapt it.

• Apr 2021 · Digital Asset raised $120M in Series D funding.

• Jun 2021 · Broadridge launched its Daml-based repo platform for short-term lending against securities.

• Nov 2021 · Broadridge CEO Tim Gokey said the repo platform was handling $35B a day.

• Mar 2022 · Digital Asset released Daml 2.0, including Canton technology for connecting applications while keeping transaction details private.

• May 2022 · SBI invested in Digital Asset and agreed to form a joint venture in Japan.

• Nov 2022 · The European Investment Bank issued a €100M digital bond on Goldman Sachs’ private, Daml-based platform.

• May 2023 · Digital Asset and other financial and technology firms announced plans to launch Canton Network.

• Sep 2023 · Yuval Rooz spoke to a U.S. House subcommittee about financial privacy and Canton.

• Oct 2023 · Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing launched Synapse, using Daml to help settle trades in mainland Chinese shares through Stock Connect.

• Jun 25, 2024 · Canton’s Global Synchronizer went live to connect applications, with transaction fees paid in Canton Coin.

• Sep 23, 2024 · DTCC and Digital Asset published results of a Canton trial using tokenized U.S. Treasuries as collateral.

• Jun 2025 · Digital Asset raised $135M in a funding round led by Tradeweb and DRW Venture Capital.

• Nov 10, 2025 · Canton Coin began trading on KuCoin.

• Nov 12, 2025 · Franklin Templeton brought Benji, its platform for tokenized investments, to Canton.

• Nov 18, 2025 · Société Générale announced its first U.S. digital bond on Canton, bought by DRW, with BNY named as paying agent.

• Dec 4, 2025 · Digital Asset announced investments from BNY, iCapital, Nasdaq and S&P Global.

• Dec 4, 2025 · USDCx, a stablecoin backed by USDC through Circle’s xReserve, went live on Canton.

• Dec 11, 2025 · SEC staff issued DTC, DTCC’s securities depository, a conditional no-action letter for its proposed tokenization service.

• Dec 17, 2025 · DTCC and Digital Asset announced plans to tokenize U.S. Treasuries held at DTC on Canton.

• Feb 18, 2026 · Canton Strategic Holdings began trading under its new Nasdaq ticker, CNTN.

• Apr 2026 · Mizuho, Nomura, Japan Securities Clearing Corporation and Digital Asset launched a trial to manage Japanese government bonds as collateral on Canton.

• Jun 2026 · Digital Asset raised $355M in a funding round led by a16z crypto.

• Jul 15, 2026 · DTCC processed live trades using tokenized securities in a limited production event ahead of its service launch.

• Jul 27, 2026 · Temple announced a Treasury-backed repo completed by DRW and HIFI on Canton, with Marex as prime broker and settlement agent.

• Aug 2026 · MUFG, Progmat and Digital Asset announced a trial of repo trades backed by Japanese government bonds on Canton.

• Sep 11, 2026 · Shinhan Asset Management received approval to participate as a Canton Super Validator.

• Sep 17, 2026 · Kyobo Life announced a completed test with SBI Digital Practice of direct yen-to-won transfers on Canton using test tokens.

• Oct 13, 2026 · Derivnex announced a completed swap between DRW and Marex on Canton, tied to a corporate bond index tokenized by Kaiko.

• Oct 28, 2026 · DTCC launched its tokenization service on Canton and its private Besu network.

• Oct 29, 2026 · Canton Strategic Holdings announced plans for tokenized CNTN shares to trade on Canton through TSV, with Fairmint as transfer agent.

• Oct 30, 2026 · HSBC announced Uber’s completed pilot using tokenized bank deposits to buy money market funds on Canton, with the ability to sell holdings over a weekend.

• Nov 2, 2026 · Société Générale announced that it had accepted $10M in tokenized U.S. Treasuries as collateral on Canton.

• Nov 3, 2026 · SEC staff said $CC was a digital commodity, based on the facts submitted, and issued a conditional no-action letter covering its automated minting.

Coin Center filed an amicus brief challenging the SDNY’s “honest validator” theory of wire fraud. In Ethereum, “honest” validation has a specific technical meaning. It does not create an open-ended legal duty to meet prosecutors’ expectations of fair play.

Had the SDNY’s theory prevailed, the government could use wire fraud law to impose its own code of conduct on Ethereum validators, backed by criminal penalties. Anyone participating in an open network would have to wonder whether prosecutors might later declare their behavior “dishonest” and haul them into court.

author: punk2898
quoted_text:
到底应该去哪里买「双币赢」？哪里的收益更高？交易所到底是怎么赚钱的？一口气跟大家讲清楚（超长干活，建议交易所同学看一下😎）

一、比特大陆和双币赢也有关系💻

第一次听说双币赢的时候，我简直惊为天人（ Callback 一下前两天的「合约拼盘😉」）

我说怎么会有人把一个复杂的金融衍生品，包装得这么简单易懂？这简直是一个天才的设计。

目前已经很难溯源到底是谁发明的，但最早大规模推广双币赢的，应该是吴忌寒的 Matrixport（以前矿机都是吴做的）

后来大概有一两年的时间，其他交易所都没有怎么跟进。因为那时候交易所太赚钱了，根本不屑于做这些衍生品（真地主家也没有余粮了）

直到后来 Binance 等交易所陆续跟进，双币赢才真正进入大众视野。

二、双币赢为什么是个好产品？🧐

大家都听过它的宣传：跌了可以抄底，涨了可以赚超额年化收益。

三、到底应该去哪里买？💰

双币赢本质上是一个期权工具，按理说，同样的标的、行权价和到期时间，各家交易所给出的收益应该大差不差。

但实际上，你去对比 OKX、Binance、Bitget、Bybit，就会发现它们之间的收益差距非常大。

为什么？

因为交易所对这个产品的定位完全不同。

📈 如果双币赢是我的主打引流款，那我就可以让出一部分利润，甚至主动补贴。

💰 如果它是我的变现款，那我就可以多赚一点。反正用户量足够大，能赚一点是一点。

这就导致同样的产品，不同交易所给出的收益完全不一样。

下面都是我的主观判断，不代表客观标准，大家参考就好。

第一，OKX：目前我认为最好的双币赢平台。

以前最好的其实是 Matrixport，没有之一。

但后来随着 FTX 爆雷，以及一系列行业事件的冲击，Matrixport 在这块的投入越来越少，现在也逐渐转向美股、港股等业务。

现在大家一提双币赢，很多人第一反应就是 OKX，但实际上这个产品并不是他们发明的。

为什么 OKX 做得最好？

我倾向于认为，它在这个产品上让出了比较多的利润，而且把双币赢收益和 VIP 等级进行了绑定。

你的 VIP 等级越高，拿到的收益就越高，甚至可能比其他交易所的普通用户高出好几个百分点。

但 OKX 真正厉害的，其实是 USDG 双币赢。

我倾向于认为，USDG 是一个超级引流款。

因为同样条件下，USDG 双币赢的收益往往比 USDT 更高，有时候能高出 10% 左右。（我不明白 OKX 为什么不宣传这个🤣）

这个差距其实相当有吸引力。

我猜测是 USDG 相关方给了一定补贴，加上 OKX 自己让出了一部分利润，才形成了这个结果。

所以在我观察的产品里，OKX 的 USDG 双币赢，目前收益是最高的，没有之一。

甚至有时候比 OKX 高等级 VIP 的其他双币赢产品还高。

第二，Binance：双币赢更偏向变现款。

你去观察 Binance 的产品布局，会发现一个很有意思的现象。

Binance 是超级头部交易所，它需要多元化发展。

除了现货、合约交易，还要有理财、衍生品等各种产品。

但它最核心的业务依然是交易。

所以我认为 Binance 对理财产品大概有两种策略。

1️⃣ 一种是用理财留住大户。

比如 U 本位理财、稳定币理财，以及各种针对大资金的产品。对于这些产品，Binance 是愿意投入资源的，因为它需要把大户留在平台上。

2️⃣ 但双币赢不太一样。

双币赢有大量散户参与，我认为 Binance 更多是把它当作一种盈利产品。

早些年我刚开始玩双币赢的时候，Binance 给出的收益真的非常差。

跟当时的 Matrixport 比，差距非常明显。

但 Binance 的用户量实在太大了，即使收益没有那么有竞争力，也有大量用户购买。

所以我认为，它在这个产品上赚了不少钱。

当然，现在 Binance 的双币赢已经比以前好很多了，只不过我依然不认为它是 Binance 最重视的核心产品。

第三，Bitget、Bybit：更重视散户运营，而不是双币赢。

Bitget 就比较有意思了。

它的双币赢有些报价其实也不错，大家看我发的截图就知道，比如 BTC 60,000 美元附近的行权价，有些产品给出的收益还是蛮高的。

但整体来看，我认为 Bitget 并没有把双币赢作为核心业务。

逻辑上也说得通。

像 OKX、Binance，这些平台有大量大户资金，所以它们会更加重视如何留住大户资产。

而 Bitget、Bybit 相对来说，更重视散户市场和运营活动。

比如更快地上线新产品、股票相关产品，以及各种热门资产。

它们更愿意把资源放在这些能够快速吸引用户的业务上。

相对而言，双币赢这种偏理财性质的衍生品，未必是它们最想投入资源的地方。

而且大户愿不愿意把大量资金长期放在这些平台，本身也是个问题。

所以你会发现，它们的运营活动很多，但双币赢的收益未必一直有竞争力。

四、最后总结一下 📝

不同平台给出的收益差异，很大程度上取决于它们到底想用这个产品来赚钱，还是用它来吸引资金。

如果是我的话，目前会优先选择 OKX 的 USDG 双币赢。

因为在我观察到的同等条件报价里，它的收益确实很有竞争力，甚至是最高的。

以上都是我的个人观察和判断，大家可以自己对比一下

手机打字，有不对的也可以指正🙏

text:
After digging deeper into this, I realized @boros_fi YU calendar spread strats are underexplored.

Also, the foundations required to trade these well are surprisingly similar to those used in options term-structure (calendar-spread) trading, especially for pricing and forecasting:

1/ Implied APR term structure
2/ Forward implied APR
3/ Forward-rate dynamics
4/ Rate sensitivity and curve risk

P.S. unlike options, Boros YUs approximately linear exposure to implied APR, rather than intrinsic convexity (excluding execution costs).

So there's no need to model \gamma, just need to identify mispriced forward funding expectations (harder than it sounds), and capturing the spread before execution cost eats away the edge.

text:
I can count on one hand the number of products where the company could take up pricing by 5-6x, and I would still gladly continue to pay for it

Claude is one of those products, and I think it speaks to just how sticky AI platforms are. When ChatGPT first came out, the switching cost felt near to zero.

Sure, there was some memory and features embedded into it. But it would take more or less no time to completely port over all the usage into something new, like Gemini, at the time

However, the same is not true today. I have seen my usage and spend go up on Claude by nearly 2-3x just in the last couple of months alone

Have built out customized skills for each of my workflows. Have fed it multiple references for how I like to format and create my excel models. Have separate custom skills for each company that I track in the public market and how to update the model after each earnings call

The product has become incredibly sticky and I don’t think I could easily switch over anymore. It would take me hours of work to build back these same custom skills and embed it into my workflow

The reason I would gladly pay, even if they were to raise prices, is because the amount of ROI I get on my time is absolutely insane

Tasks like updating a model for quarterly earnings might have taken couple hours before. Now that takes about 10 minutes at most.

This is not a 10-20% efficiency gain tool. I am talking step changes in productivity and output. Absolutely love the product. Don’t say that about many things anymore

text:
Lighter 这次被攻击的链路，按推断是这样的：

- 攻击者拿到被盗账户 A 的交易 API key，用它创建了一个属于 A 的vault。
- 攻击者用自己的账户 B 申购这个vault，拿到绝大部分份额。
- 攻击者再用 A 的 API key（被泄漏了），把 A 账户里的钱充进vault（最大的问题在这里）。这笔充值不增加份额，所以 B 依然持有绝大部分份额，但池子里的钱变多了。
- B 赎回份额，就能把 A 后来充进去的钱一起提走。

如果这条链路得到确认，Lighter 这次被盗就有两层问题：一个是 API key 被泄漏；另一个是trading API key 居然可以往vault里充钱。

后者是一个巨大的设计漏洞。用户授权 API 做交易，不等于授权它把自己的钱放进别人持有份额的池子，让别人赎回拿走。即使没有直接提现权限，也能达到转走资产的效果。

任何资产受益权的变更，都不应该绕过资金所有者明确授予的权限。

API Key 泄露应该是安全系统必须考虑的威胁模型，$15.5M 的教训，不应该只是一句“请用户轮换 API Key”。
